Pope Leo XIV waves from the window of the car as he leaves the Vatican before being admitted to Rome’s Gemelli University Hospital for an operation to remove a lump from his lung, in the Vatican on 13 October 2026. — AFP pic
‘Thoughts and prayers’
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a practising Catholic, said after the surgery that he and his wife were “united in prayer for (Leo’s) health following his recent diagnosis”.
“May the Lord give him strength and the Holy Spirit guide the medical professionals taking care of the Holy Father,” Rubio said on X.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said his “thoughts and prayers” were with the pontiff, calling him “a voice for peace, humanity and reason in our modern world”.
Leo had entered the hospital smiling and waving earlier yesterday hours before the surgery.
He is staying in a room on the 10th floor of the building, next to a papal suite with a private chapel that is currently under renovation.
The Vatican has said it expects the recovery to take a week.
His audiences have been cancelled until October 20 and the operation raises questions about whether the pope will go on a lengthy visit to Latin America next month.
The surgery marks Leo’s first hospitalisation since he became head of the Catholic Church on May 8, 2025.
In a surprise announcement following Angelus prayers on Sunday, Leo told crowds in St Peter’s Square that doctors had discovered a nodule “at a very early stage” during medical checks.
“The doctors believe it would be right to intervene,” he said.

The Vatican has historically been very secretive about the health of popes, but began to be more transparent during the illness of Leo’s predecessor Francis, an Argentine who freely discussed his ailments.
Ahead of the operation, people outside the hospital expressed concern over the pope’s condition.
Giorgia Fei, a 57-year-old Italian, said she had been worried.
“However, the Holy Father is in very good hands here at the hospital because we have some outstanding doctors,” she said.
“I will pray a lot for him.”
Giuseppe Purpura, 72, said he too was concerned.
“He’s still quite young and I really wasn’t expecting this. I thought he was in better health,” he said, noting that “thankfully it was caught in time”.
Latin America trip in doubt
The Vicar General for the Diocese of Rome, Cardinal Baldassare Reina, led a rosary prayer for the pope inside the hospital chapel which was broadcast by the Vatican.
Dozens of people attended, and Reina asked all the city’s parishes to join in.
The Vatican secretary of state, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, told ANSA news agency that Leo had been “very calm” about his condition when they met on Monday.
The Vatican told AFP the nodule was found during routine health checks, and there were no symptoms that led to checking the pope’s lungs.
Chicago-born Leo, the first US pope, is sporty and believed to generally be in good health.
He is scheduled to travel to South America from November 6-17 to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. — AFP
9e12dbe54c3d3d77: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 14 — A dramatic video capturing the terrifying moment violent storm winds appeared to lift a car and toss it into another vehicle near a toll plaza in Kota Damansara has gone viral on social media.

The footage, shared online at around 6.30pm yesterday, shows what witnesses described as a waterspout or freak whirlwind striking motorists queuing along the toll lanes amid blinding rain and howling gusts.

423e0870abdf794e: NEW YORK: Cornell University on Tuesday suspended fraternities' parties and social events for the remaining academic year following outcry over an alleged gang rape at one of the elite college's all-male clubs.
The 2024 incident, as alleged in a graphic lawsuit filed last month, has drawn accusations that the Ivy League institution in New York state failed to properly punish the men involved.
The accuser claimed that she was pressured to take ketamine, assaulted and raped by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity -- one of several "Greek life" organisations common across US colleges.
Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff said the suspension "will provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue."
"I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024, and appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community," he added, referring to the accuser's pseudonym.
Following her initial allegations, Cornell shut down the fraternity and temporarily suspended the accused male students, two of whom were later expelled.
But critics have said the university's response was too lenient, prompting it to launch an independent review.
Thousands of students and faculty members rallied at Cornell this month to demand justice for the accuser, displaying signs reading "Hold them accountable" and "Protect survivors."
Protesters have also gathered in New York, Boston and other US cities to show support for the accuser, while social media users have shared the hashtag #IAmJaneDoe on TikTok, X and Instagram.
Cornell has named a former top US prosecutor, Sally Yates, to assess the university's response to the rape allegations.
But, addressing the Cornell community, Kotlikoff said Tuesday "it is clear that we cannot wait for these findings to take action."
He said the suspension on fraternity social events was effective immediately and there would be "zero tolerance" for any violations.
"Any fraternity holding an in-house party or social event will receive an immediate emergency suspension," Kotlikoff said.

He announced other measures including the appointment of a dedicated staff member to support individuals reporting sexual misconduct, and inviting specialized New York State Police detectives to probe future sexual assault allegations.
Meanwhile, prosecutors have reopened an investigation into the alleged gang rape, with Governor Kathy Hochul appointing state Attorney General Letitia James to lead the case.
That came after local authorities said they declined to prosecute in 2024 because the complainant's testimony did not establish a lack of consent.

In the US, one in four female undergraduates experienced forced sexual contact or sexual contact for which they could not consent, according to a 2020 study of 33 institutions by the Association of American Universities.
Mental health nonprofit the Jed Foundation has reported that men in fraternities -- which are routinely criticized for shielding sexism -- are more likely to commit sexual violence.
f7d094a6b6b2b593: LETTER: At what age is someone officially considered as a senior citizen - 55, 60, 62 or 65? The answer depends on where you are and what you are paying for.
Malaysia's National Policy for Older Persons defines an older person as someone aged 60 and above. Yet the tourism and leisure businesses do not apply the same threshold consistently.
Golden Screen Cinemas, for example, offers senior citizen rates to patrons aged 55 years old and above. Penang Hill and Sunway Lagoon use 60, while Petrosains places senior admission at 61 and above.

The differences are not unique to Malaysia. In the United States, the National Park Service offers its Senior Pass from 62 years old, while English Heritage in Britain provides senior concession tickets from 65.
So there is clearly no universal age at which a tourist suddenly becomes "senior".
Chronological age alone does not tell us about whether a person is healthy, active, financially independent or physically restricted.
This matters as Malaysia's population ages. People in their late 55s or early 60s today may be very different from someone of the same age several decades ago.
Many continue working, travelling and participating actively in leisure. Others may experience mobility, health or financial constraints earlier.
Should Malaysia therefore lower all senior discounts to 55? Not necessarily.
A blanket rule could increase costs for attractions and reduce ticket revenue, particularly for operators already providing substantial concessions. Age alone also does not indicate financial need.

But, the current situation deserves another look. Instead of requiring every attraction to adopt the same age, the tourism industry could distinguish between an official senior citizen entitlement and a senior tourism market.
The official threshold of 60 could remain for government related concessions.
Tourism businesses, however, could have the flexibility to recognise the broader 55 plus market through off peak discounts, weekday promotions, loyalty programmes or special packages.
This could benefit both sides. Senior tourists may be encouraged to travel more frequently, while attractions could attract visitors during quieter periods.
They may also benefit from spending on food, retail, transport and family members travelling together.
More importantly, senior friendly tourism should not end with a cheaper ticket.
Accessible toilets, seating areas, safe walkways, clear information, simple digital booking and helpful staff may matter far more than saving a few ringgit.

Malaysia therefore does not necessarily need one compulsory age for every senior discount but greater clarity over what "senior" means, why a concession is being offered and whom it is intended to help.
LIEW SIEN LEONG
Lecturer
School of Tourism, Hospitality and Event Management
Universiti Utara Malaysia

7a1715d903e69949: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 14 — Legislation to curb “Alibaba” licensing practices, Malaysia’s diplomatic efforts on Gaza and the fate of an abandoned housing project are among the key issues expected to be raised in the Dewan Rakyat today.

According to the Order Paper, Syahredzan Johan (PH-Bangi) will ask the Economy Minister about the status of drafting the Anti-Rent-Seeking Act and the timeline for its tabling in Parliament to curb “Alibaba” licensing practices.

The West Asia conflict is also expected to feature prominently, with Ahmad Tarmizi Sulaiman (PN-Sik) asking the Foreign Minister about Malaysia’s diplomatic efforts at the United Nations (UN) and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) to ensure that the ceasefire and humanitarian aid to Gaza continue.

Also drawing attention is the fate of 1,120 residential units at the Residensi Wilayah Salak Selatan apartment project, with Fong Kui Lun (PH-Bukit Bintang) asking the Housing and Local Government Ministry to explain its rescue plan, including a proposal to appoint a rescue developer if the Scheme of Arrangement fails.

Meanwhile, Jimmy Puah Wee Tse (PH-Tebrau) will raise preparations for workforce transition plans in response to the threat posed by artificial intelligence (AI), while Suhaizan Kaiat (PH-Pulai) will ask about median wages and graduates working in jobs below their academic qualifications (underemployment).

Other matters on the agenda include the future direction of the Tabung Pahlawan, with Nordin Ahmad Ismail (PN-Lumut) asking the Defence Minister to explain its transformation; the distribution of aid to Sekolah Agama Rakyat in 2026, raised by Datuk Ahmad Saad @ Yahaya (PN-Pokok Sena); and agricultural input costs and bushfires on Pulau Bruit, Sarawak, raised by Sabri Azit (PN-Jerai).
After the question-and-answer session, the Dewan Rakyat will consider a motion to appoint Members of Parliament to the Parliamentary Services Council, to be tabled by the Prime Minister.

Under the motion, two government MPs, Ramkarpal Singh (PH-Bukit Gelugor) and Datuk Seri Hasni Mohammad (BN-Simpang Renggam), and two opposition MPs, Datuk Seri Dr Ronald Kiandee (PN-Beluran) and Datuk Seri Takiyuddin Hassan (PN-Kota Bharu), will be nominated to serve on the council in accordance with Section 3(2)(f) of the Parliamentary Services Act 2025.

The Dewan Rakyat will then continue debating the Supply Bill 2027 at the policy stage, following the tabling of Budget 2027 by Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim, who is also Finance Minister, last Friday.

According to the calendar for the Third Meeting of the Fifth Session of the 15th Parliament, the policy-stage debate on Budget 2027 runs from October 12 to 22, before ministers deliver their winding-up speeches over four days beginning October 26.
The Dewan Rakyat sitting runs for 37 days until December 8. — Bernama
0f6a0f8d959c48ae: KUALA LUMPUR: The Immigration Department has identified 224 hotspots nationwide linked to the presence and activities of foreigners, including illegal settlements and overcrowded rental houses.
Immigration director-general Datuk Zakaria Shaaban said other locations included workers' quarters at construction sites and business premises dominated by foreigners.
He said these locations required close attention and enforcement monitoring.

"From 2023 to June 15 this year, a total of 16,431 Op Sapu operations were conducted. These operations involved raids on various illegal settlements, including squatter houses, workers' quarters and lodging houses found to be occupied by undocumented migrants.
"During the period, 50,382 foreigners were detained for various offences under the Immigration Act," he said in an exclusive interview.
Zakaria said a location's status as a hotspot was not fixed but subject to ongoing assessment based on intelligence, public complaints, findings from enforcement operations and current analysis.
The assessment also took into account changes in the patterns of foreigners' presence, intelligence findings and enforcement action, he added.

"The department will continue to carry out targeted, intelligence-led enforcement while strengthening cooperation with local authorities and enforcement agencies within their respective jurisdictions.
"Action will also be taken against employers and other parties that employ or shelter undocumented migrants, or facilitate their presence, in accordance with the law," he said.
Zakaria said illegal settlements and villages involved the jurisdictions of several parties, including local authorities and other agencies.
"Within the department's jurisdiction, enforcement focuses on foreigners who are in the country in violation of immigration laws.
"As such, enforcement does not end once an operation has been carried out.

"Monitoring and enforcement will continue based on information, complaints and intelligence, including through strategic cooperation with local authorities and other enforcement agencies to address the presence of undocumented migrants at identified locations," he said.

He said the department also prioritised action against parties contributing to the presence of undocumented migrants, including employers who hired them or parties who sheltered them or allowed them to stay on their premises.
These included employers hiring undocumented migrants and parties sheltering them or allowing them to remain on their premises, subject to the provisions of the law in force.
"This approach is strengthened through intelligence, data analysis and information-sharing between agencies to identify high-risk locations and enable more targeted and sustained enforcement.

"Addressing this issue requires a comprehensive, inter-agency approach, not only through operations against undocumented migrants but also by tackling the factors that enable them to remain and work illegally in the country," he said.
428004c7a70e54d4: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 14 — Most establishments opened by Chinese expatriates in Malaysia often feature a mix of cuisines from all over China, capturing a small part of what they enjoy back in China.
This Taman Danau Desa establishment is operated by two generations of a family originally from Shenyang, a city in Northeast China.
Come here for their roujiamo or “meat in a bun,” a popular Xi’an street snack that is essentially a Chinese-style hamburger.

Variations of roujiamo exist with different buns and fillings but this place serves the Tongguan variety, which uses a thousand-layer bun that is crispy and flaky, making it stand out compared to a normal pocket size piece of bread.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
This is the Tongguan version with the round flatbread that has crispy, flaky layers paired with either pork or beef — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
As you crunch down on the round flatbread with paper-thin layers, you reach the fatty meat filling mixed with chopped coriander that oozes with its juices, providing an unexpected surprise.
The flaky wonder comes with a pork filling (RM11) or a beef version (RM13); the pork version oozes sweet juices, while the beef one has a noticeably meatier flavour.
Be warned: one bite of flaky-crunchy-juiciness will hook you for seconds.
Typically in Xi’an, locals pair roujiamo with Handmade Sesame Cold Noodles (RM11) or knife-cut Liang Pi with a bottle of orange-flavoured soda called Bing Feng or Ice Peak.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Handmade Sesame Cold Noodles are made daily with wide ribbons paired with a sesame sauce, cucumber, bean sprouts and chili — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
Made in-house daily, the cold noodles, which resemble wide ribbons, are tangled with sesame sauce, thinly cut cucumber, bean sprouts and starchy wheat gluten.
In Xi’an, the palate leans more sour-and-hot, which wakes up the appetite.

I’ve sampled boiled dumplings paired with vinegar and thin shreds of ginger or pan-fried versions but this combination of Dumplings in Sour Soup (RM14) elevates those hand-folded nuggets of pork and vegetables encased in smooth skin.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Dumplings in Sour Soup is an appetising way to enjoy boiled dumplings filled with pork and vegetables — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
Amidst the sourness, you find an unlikely companion of seaweed in the soup, which imparts a silky softness.
Don’t miss out on their Crispy Sweet & Sour Pork (RM27), their version of the iconic Guo You Rou, the Dongbei version of sweet and sour pork.
It features large slices of pork tenderloin, not the small pieces typically used in sweet and sour pork.
These slices are coated in potato starch and deep fried to a golden crust with bubbles that threaten to burst.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Crispy Sweet & Sour Pork features thin pork tenderloin slices paired with a sugar-rice vinegar sauce that will have you asking for more — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
No tomato sullies this dish. Instead it’s a simple mix of rice vinegar and sugar, which takes on a golden brown hue from the sesame oil.
Here, soymilk is freshly made, pulling you with the satiny goodness from the soy beans.

It’s also coagulated into smooth, wobbly soymilk custard laced with sweet syrup (RM4.50) — the typical flavour pairing — but spring for the Savoury Tofu Hua (RM5) with a velvety sauce and a dollop of chili sauce for a different flavour.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
We only know the sweet version but try the Savoury Tofu Hua, a wobbly soybean milk custard paired with chili sauce — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
Familiar classics pepper the menu, which are popular with many like the fish slices served with pickled vegetables or Sichuan peppercorns.

Quick and easy meals for one can also be ordered, such as different rice bowls topped with tomato and egg, braised eggplant, diced chicken with chili, and the Stir-Fried Spicy Tofu Rice Bowl (RM14) which is their version of mapo tofu.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Various rice bowls catering to solo diners can be ordered like this Stir-Fried Spicy Tofu Rice Bowl — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
The beancurd is diced and cooked with a spicy, deep flavour of Sichuan chilli bean paste and fermented black beans, making white rice an essential accompaniment.
For a finish that isn’t too sweet — the way many Chinese prefer — there’s Golden Fried Glutinous Red Bean Cake (RM3.50).
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Golden Fried Glutinous Red Bean Cake (left) is a chewy not-too-sweet dessert. The restaurant (right) is hidden in a quieter area within Taman Danau Desa Business Centre — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
The slightly chewy mochi-like glutinous rice cake contains red bean paste and is best enjoyed with a cup of hot tea as you wind down a meal here.
Fortune Cafe
Taman Danau Desa Business Centre,
Taman Desa, Kuala Lumpur.
Open daily: 10.30am to 10pm

251571a6880be567: OCTOBER 14 — I spent a night playing Magic: The Gathering (MTG) at a little gaming store that was just a short train ride away from me.
Adventurer's Hall is a few metres away from the Taman Bahagia station on the first floor of an unassuming shoplot, with a paper sign on the stairway door grille.
I was there only because Facebook showed me a post saying it was an all femme MTG night and after meeting the Mana Coven, an all female MTG group at a recent event, I was somewhat intrigued.
Also, I really needed to learn how to play the very popular MTG format, Commander.
MTG started out as a two-player game. The premise of it is that you are planewalkers or basically, wizards, duelling with spells and creatures, all this done via cards.
"Oh just like Harry Potter."
Please do not mention that franchise to me, especially now that JK Rowling has declared she will spend her earnings on her anti-trans activism.
Why couldn't she be like Enya who made her millions and now just shuts herself up in a literal castle with her cats and is blissfully not on social media?
Commander however is a different format — you play in groups of two to four people and the objective is to be the last planeswalker standing.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Tabletop gaming is now a lot more accessible than it used to be. — Picture by Erna Mahyuni
Harry Potter-rants aside I wasn't sure what I'd experience when I arrived at Adventurer's Hall but it was a very chill old kopitiam-vibe.
A menu with finger food, a couple of separate rooms with tables, a Warhammer display, Dungeons & Dragons books and of course a counter with MTG cards.
One random dude misunderstood the theme of the Commander session and thought the "Femme" thing was a Lord of the Rings reference.
He ended up joining another group to play boardgames so all's well that ends well.
My "pod" for the night as they call them apparently these days consisted of two other lovely women, one a Master's student and another who worked in tech.
They both absolutely trampled my deck but it was a good learning experience and I look forward to being stomped on as I continue learning MTG.
My current limitation for MTG is that I am strictly only buying or getting products from the newly-released Reality Fracture set because otherwise I will not be eating.
As many of you know, I really do love food.

Adventurer's Hall, I found out later, is run by a group of friends who all have day jobs but run it as a part-time endeavour (though one of them is going to make it his fulltime pursuit due to, well, reasons).
It has been nearly two decades since I stepped away from tabletop gaming, besides playing board games (that aren't Monopoly) and it's been interesting seeing how the hobby has expanded.
The commodification of trading card games might have somewhat contributed to the scene and the frenzy for Pokémon cards thanks to influencers.
At Adventurer's Hall, though, it was a bunch of people just having some fun either participating in roleplaying game sessions or card games.
It reminded me of two decades prior when I spent my nights hanging out at a game store, watching people paint Warhammer figures, play MTG (of course) and making friends.
One of those friends is now my housemate and colleague, and one of my dearest friends.
Quite a few of the people I met in those days are now my friends on Facebook too.
I don't want to revisit nostalgia by picking up MTG now; the game has changed, as have the players.
Just like before, though, I'll watch and learn, about people, about games, about life in general.
The MTG set Reality Fracture is about a wizard trying to remake the world and remove all suffering, but ends up creating more suffering as his new universe devours the old one.

It is a strange parallel to our current times where tech bros are trying to remake the world by replacing talent and thought with randomised word generators, claiming it will lead to prosperity for all.
While in reality, the forests are burning, our reservoirs are drying up, GPUs cost the same as cars or a house downpayment and the world as we know it is being gobbled up by private equity.
Anyway I'm not getting paid for this but you can check out the events at Adventurers' Hall on their very shiny website.
Maybe I'll see you there — I'll be the half-blind middle-aged woman squinting at the too-small text on her MTG cards.
* This is the personal opinion of the columnist.

dadc798f1a763024: MANCHESTER: Paris Saint-Germain coach Luis Enrique said Manchester City "deserve" the trophies they won on the pitch and hopes the English side avoid sanction despite being found guilty of breaking the Premier League's financial rules.
City face severe sanctions, including potential relegation from English football's top-flight, after an independent commission found them guilty on over 100 charges between 2009 and 2018.
There has also been speculation that titles won during that period could be stripped.
City have appealed the verdict and deny any wrongdoing.
Former City boss Pep Guardiola, who left the club in May, is set to return to the Etihad for Wednesday's clash against PSG in the Champions League.
Luis Enrique is a close friend and former Barcelona teammate of Guardiola and said what City won on the field should not be taken away from them.

"I think what they've done on the pitch has been incredible over the last few years and I think they certainly deserve to win on the pitch all the trophies that they have won," the PSG boss said in a pre-match press conference.
"I think the trophies that you win on the pitch remains on the pitch and they deserve to win. I hope they can avoid that sanction, that's what I feel."
Enzo Maresca has so far made a flawless start to the daunting task of succeeding Guardiola.
The Italian has won all eight games in all competitions, but Luis Enrique dismissed suggestions Wednesday's match is the chance to lay down an early marker for either side.
"January is when you can really see the team's level," he added. "Five or six months down the line, things are so different. Many teams change.
"But it's an interesting match at this stage, a fun one to watch."

f906b803e3fa3d76: Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s Budget 2027 address did not disappoint, transforming fiscal data into an intellectual narrative, and breathing life into the ledger by anchoring it in philosophy.

In tabling the Supply Bill on Oct 9, he assembled a jury of philosophers, poets, and thinkers from five civilisations and asked them to testify. He sought their assistance in telling Malaysians that a budget is not merely arithmetic but a covenant—and that covenants are owed to the future. Everything else in the speech is scaffolding around that claim.
Anwar opened with lighad (“for tomorrow”) from Surah al-Hashr (59:18), establishing intergenerational obligation as a religious duty before it becomes a fiscal one.

He said: “True progress is measured not by how far we travel, but by what we carry together along the way: human dignity, strong families, a fair chance for each generation to rise, the integrity of our institutions, and the conviction that effort will be repaid with opportunity. It is not enough to inherit our strengths. We must enlarge them, until they become a greater legacy for those who follow.”
He then introduced British philosopher Isaiah Berlin’s hedgehog and the fox image: a nation needs "one big thing" held steadily (its ambition) and many things known flexibly (its methods).
“The fox knows many things; the hedgehog knows one big thing. A nation needs both. A nation must hold to one great and constant ambition: a purpose that gives the journey its direction and meaning.”
Immediately after, tenth-century jurist Al-Mawardi established that power cannot stand without order, law, and responsibility.
This was paired with the classical Malay poet Raja Ali Haji’s Gurindam Dua Belas (1847), anchoring the bond between ruler and ruled in waad—a covenant.

“In our tradition, the bond between those who govern and those who are governed has never rested on power alone. It is anchored in waad – a covenant, in which loyalty must be answered with justice, and power must be fenced in by trust.”

The American philosopher John Rawls then performed the heaviest analytical lifting, deploying it at exactly the right moment. After announcing differentiated allocations to states, Anwar anticipated accusations of favouritism and relied on equity rather than uniform treatment:

"That is how we have approached allocations to the states. Developed states can keep surging ahead. Developing states get room to pick up the pace... That is what equity means: not every state getting the same, but every state getting what is fair and reasonable."

Although invoking Rawlsian-adjacent logic provided a philosophical wrapper for inter-governmental distribution, applying it directly glossed over the complex constitutional debates of federal funding formulas. Yet, the rhetoric served its purpose.

Next, Tamil poet-philosopher Thiruvalluvar’s Thirukkural (couplet 731)—which describes a good country as having adequate food production, learned citizens and honest businessmen - arrived just before a RM69 billion education allocation, including RM50 million for Tamil primary schools.
Likewise, a Tang-dynasty monk's verse (Shangtang Kaishi Song) on the plum blossom enduring bitter cold was placed right before fiscal sacrifice and subsidy rationalisation were addressed.
Homer closed the arc. Odysseus braves storms yet never loses his unwavering memory of Ithaca:
"Every nation must know its Ithaca: the ambition it seeks, the values and roots it will defend, and the legacy it means to leave."
Anwar returned to lighad at the close, sealing the ring.

This was no random name-dropping. It was a deliberate comparative theology of governance. Anwar treated the Quran, the Tirukkural, Homer, and Rawls not as conflicting authorities, but as different dialects of the same moral language.

Justice, foresight, and institutional integrity were framed not as Western, Islamic, Indian, Chinese, or Malay monopolies, but as universal human aspirations - a potent message for a multi-ethnic society.
By framing fiscal decisions through a civilisational lens, Anwar attempted to elevate fiscal discipline from a technical necessity to a moral imperative.

One might be tempted to see this as an effort to depoliticise the budget but that risks oversimplifying domestic realpolitik. Rather than neutralising politics, the rhetoric attempted to reshape the terms of political engagement, lifting the conversation above mere transactional patronage.
Anwar’s rhetoric was undeniably ambitious. He wanted Malaysians to see the budget as the fulfillment of a shared moral contract.
Yet, a tension remains.
The intention is to unify, but the ultimate success depends on whether economic benefits are tangibly felt across all communities.

In the end, this covenant will not be weighed in the Dewan Rakyat, but in the lives of the rakyat. If this pluralist vision translates into equitable prosperity, Anwar’s citations will be remembered as the blueprint for a new Malaysia. If not, they will be seen as just beautiful words without substance.

0750f3692c5f6d4e: KUALA KANGSAR: Every morning, 75-year-old Jahara Hashim gets on her bicycle and rides for about 30 minutes from Kampung Changkat Manong to the Senior Citizens Activity Centre in Manong. She has diabetes and high blood pressure, and has lived alone since her husband died 22 years ago.
Her two children are married and have repeatedly asked her to move in with them, but Jahara prefers to remain in her own home.
What she does not want, however, is to spend her days there by herself.

For the past five years, she has arrived at the centre by 8am and usually returns home at about 1pm. The routine gives her somewhere to go, friends to talk to and, perhaps just as importantly, people who would notice if she suddenly stopped turning up.
“My children do worry about me. They tell me to just rest at home in case anything happens to me,” she told Bernama. “But staying at home can be boring.”

Her children call regularly and visit every week, while friends at the centre also know her habits well enough to spot when something is amiss. That combination of independence and connection is becoming increasingly important as Malaysia’s population ages.
When nobody notices

Cases in which people die alone at home and are discovered only days later have become increasingly visible in local news reports. The phenomenon is often associated with Japan, where the term "kodokushi", or “lonely death”, is commonly used for people who die alone and remain undiscovered for an extended period.
In Malaysia, the issue is not confined to the elderly. People in their 30s and 40s have also been found dead alone at home, according to the Perak fire and rescue department.
Its director, Sayani Saidon, said the department recorded 15 such cases in the state between 2021 and July this year. Four were recorded in 2025, with another four between January and July 2026.

In many of the cases, firefighters were called by police or members of the public to gain entry into locked homes. Some of the bodies had already begun decomposing, and several people were believed to have been dead for more than a week.
Sayani noted that more older people are now living alone as adult children move elsewhere for work or as families become smaller and more geographically dispersed.

The risk for them is not simply loneliness: a person who falls, becomes suddenly unwell or loses consciousness at home may not be able to call for help, particularly if nobody nearby is aware of their usual routine.
Why Perak is especially vulnerable

Perak has the highest proportion of residents aged 65 and above in Malaysia. According to the statistics department, 10.8% of the state’s 2.58 million residents are aged 65 and older, while 15.3% are 60 and above.

Those numbers matter because ageing can bring a greater risk of chronic illness, reduced mobility, falls and loss of muscle strength. None of these inevitably prevents someone from living independently, but they can make social contact and regular check-ins more important.

For many older Malaysians, living alone is also a choice rather than a sign of neglect. They may feel comfortable in familiar surroundings, value their independence or simply prefer the routines they have built over decades.
Jahara is one example. She does not want to leave her home, but she has created a daily rhythm that keeps her connected to others.

That distinction matters because the real vulnerability is not necessarily living alone, but living alone without anyone noticing a change in routine. Sayani said families who live far from ageing parents should maintain regular contact and know how to reach a nearby neighbour if something seems wrong.

Neighbours, meanwhile, can play a role simply by being aware of those around them. This can be especially important for older residents and people with chronic health problems who may need help quickly if something happens at home.
Staying connected - and physically capable

For older people, maintaining independence also depends partly on physical health. Perak’s senior-citizen programmes have begun paying closer attention to sarcopenia, the gradual loss of muscle mass, strength and function that can occur with age.

The condition can make ordinary tasks such as climbing stairs, carrying groceries or getting up after a fall increasingly difficult. Health screening, strength-building exercise and adequate nutrition can help older adults better understand and preserve their physical capabilities.

But physical fitness is only one part of healthy ageing. Regular activities outside the home can also provide structure, companionship and something less easily measured: the reassurance that somebody knows you are there.
For Jahara, that network exists in the simplest of ways. She rides her bicycle to the same place each morning, spends several hours among familiar faces and heads home again after lunch.
And if one morning she does not arrive, someone is likely to notice.
9dd9087e03cb4878: PETALING JAYA: Ahmad Maslan gembira Barisan Nasional (BN) diramal menang besar pada PRN Melaka namun mengingatkan parti tidak terlalu yakin menjelang hari mengundi 14 Nov.

dc07511c2460e54f: WASHINGTON: Does cooking for members of a Nigerian separatist group amount to providing "material support" for terrorism?
That's the thorny question facing the conservative-majority US Supreme Court.

In a brief order Tuesday, the Supreme Court agreed to hear the Trump administration's bid to reinstate the ruling that denied asylum to a Nigerian man who was deported for having provided material support to a terrorist group.
The case will be considered during the Court's current term, which began Oct 5 and runs through late June.

Beyond Izuchukwu Ozurumba's case, the ruling could have far-reaching implications for asylum seekers, depending largely on how the nine justices – six conservatives and three liberals – interpret the concept of "material support."
Izuchukwu Ozurumba says he was forced to cook for about six months at a separatist group's camp in southern Nigeria beginning in 2022.
He then fled to Venezuela and from there crossed the US-Mexico border illegally in the summer of 2023.

In 2024, a US immigration judge denied Ozurumba's asylum claim and ordered him deported citing a provision of US immigration law that bars foreign nationals who provide "material support" to a terrorist organisation from receiving asylum.
The decision was later upheld on appeal.
Ozurumba was deported to Nigeria in April 2025, according to his lawyers.
But a federal appeals court later overturned the earlier decisions and sent the case back to the immigration court for reconsideration.

"Cooking meals using food and supplies purchased by the organization may have 'sustained' the organization in the broadest possible sense...but provided nothing that the organization could use or readily divert to plan or carry out its terrorist activities," the appeals court wrote.
"As far as the record shows, Ozurumba was simply a captive labourer whose work had nothing to do with those activities."
The Trump administration, as part of its sweeping campaign of deportations of undocumented immigrants, is asking the Supreme Court to overturn the appeals court ruling.
9537e8887f16568e: KUALA LUMPUR: Legislation to curb "Ali Baba" licensing practices, Malaysia's diplomatic efforts to sustain the Gaza ceasefire and the fate of a troubled housing project are among the key issues expected to be raised in the Dewan Rakyat today.

The fate of 1,120 residential units at the abandoned Residensi Wilayah Salak Selatan apartment project is another key issue, with Fong Kui Lun (PH-Bukit Bintang) asking the Housing and Local Government Ministry to explain its rescue plan, including a proposal to appoint a rescue developer if the Scheme of Arrangement fails.

Jimmy Puah (PH-Tebrau) will raise preparations for workforce transition plans in response to the challenges posed by artificial intelligence, while Suhaizan Kaiat (PH-Pulai) will ask about median wages and graduate underemployment, particularly those working in jobs below their qualifications.

3c94a2925ee60deb: SINGAPORE: Singapore's central bank on Wednesday kept its monetary policy settings unchanged.

65fd92382f025ffa: NEW YORK: Gold prices edged lower on Tuesday, while investors awaited key US inflation data and remarks from the Federal Reserve chair due later this week to gauge the outlook on monetary policy.
Spot gold fell 0.3 per cent to US$4,157.90 per ounce by 2.15pm EDT (1815 GMT). US gold futures for December settled down 0.3 per cent at US$4,177.30 per ounce.
"We have some inflation data that's coming out later this week. So market is kind of waiting to see how that plays out," said Bob Haberkorn, senior market strategist at StoneX.
He noted the Fed chairman will deliver his last speech before the upcoming rate meeting on Thursday, and anticipates a quieter session ahead of Wednesday's and Thursday's events.
Investors are looking ahead to the Consumer Price Index data on Wednesday, while Thursday's Producer Price Index figures and remarks from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh will be closely parsed.
Fed Governor Christopher Waller on Tuesday said the recent rise in US bond yields reflects stronger economic growth rather than higher inflation expectations, which remain "well anchored".
Gold loses its appeal in a high-interest-rate environment as it does not yield interest.

While higher rates raise the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding assets such as gold, they also intensify the fiscal burden on many governments and thereby exacerbate debt sustainability concerns," analysts at Commerzbank said in a note.

5ac9a9600d72647c: NEW YORK: Wall Street stocks were mostly lower at the end of a choppy session Tuesday, digesting solid results from US banks and a pullback in Asian markets prompted by worries over the AI investment boom.
While JPMorgan Chase missed analyst estimates, the US banking giant joined three other large US banks in reporting year-on-year profit increases that pointed to continued health in the US consumer.

JPMorgan Chief Financial Officer Jeremy Barnum described US consumer spending as "sort of robust," adding that the consumer credit picture remains "quite resilient" despite persistent inflationary trends.

The strong bank earnings gave some support to Wall Street indices, although investors remained cautious ahead of Wednesday's consumer price index data, a key input to upcoming Federal Reserve decisions.
"Any real acceleration (in inflation) would probably send yields back up, the dollar back up, and that could be a problem for equities," said Peter Cardillo of Spartan Capital Securities.
The S&P 500 finished essentially flat, while both the Dow and Nasdaq ended modestly lower.
Earlier, Asian equity markets were under renewed pressure due to weakness in AI-related names.
The selling came after Hock Tan, chief executive of the US semiconductor giant Broadcom, likened the AI buying frenzy to gambling.

"A lot of investors have no clue what they are investing in," Tan told a conference in Singapore, saying they "set very extreme expectations only to find out that it's almost like they are in a casino".
The International Monetary Fund weighed in on the debate, warning of an AI correction at the beginning of its annual meeting in Bangkok.

The boom in artificial intelligence -- and the related rush to manufacture semiconductors and build data centres -- has provided a boost to global growth despite geopolitical pressures including the Middle East war.

But "growing evidence suggests that AI capabilities can be delivered at lower investment levels... or that potential economic gains may not be as large as expected", the IMF said in its Global Financial Stability Report.
On the trading floors, South Korea's Kospi index tanked 5.5 per cent by the close as chip titans SK hynix and Samsung took a beating.

The company is aiming to release a new server-memory product based on the structure by the end of the year, the reports said.

ba03290e5b6b2a60: LONDON/SINGAPORE: Oil prices were mixed on Tuesday as hopes the US-Russia diesel deal could free up more supplies from Moscow offset attacks in Saudi Arabia and Yemen that could result in additional supply disruptions.

MIDDLE EAST ATTACKS

Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis said Saudi Arabia was attacking the Yemeni capital Sanaa on Tuesday after a Saudi-led coalition warned civilians to stay away from an oil depot on the city outskirts, part of a rapidly escalating war between the sides.

Loud booms were heard in the vicinity of Saudi Aramco's headquarters in Dhahran, six sources told Reuters.

ed21c423ffc3b078: WASHINGTON: Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook's lawyer has questioned the objectivity of a White House probe into allegations that she committed mortgage fraud, according to a letter seen by Reuters on Tuesday, challenging President Donald Trump's latest attempt to remove her from her role.

Trump has been trying to fire Cook for more than a year as he moves to exert more control over a central bank he says is refusing to lower interest rates for political reasons. Cook denies any wrongdoing and has sued to keep her job.

Earlier this month, Trump announced a fresh inquiry into Cook and the appointment of a three-person committee to hold a hearing. The president later told reporters he would proceed with her firing if the committee recommended it. Cook's lawyers have said a fair hearing would show there was no legal basis for firing her.

In Tuesday's letter, Cook's lawyer, Abbe Lowell, noted that one of the proposed committee members, White House economic policy adviser Kevin Hassett, had previously pressured Cook to take leave from her post and suggested Trump had "cause" to fire her.

"A hearing with demonstrably biased members, unspecified additional allegations, and an unclear schedule for the disclosure of any additional evidence — with no explanation for why it was not previously produced — is not a process that respects the appearance or history of independence," Lowell wrote.

Lowell said Cook would not be able to attend a hearing on Nov 5, the date announced by the White House, because she would be fulfilling her duties in Europe "at financial and monetary policy meetings".
The earliest Cook could attend any hearing would be after the Fed's policy meeting scheduled for Dec 8-9, he wrote.

A Supreme Court ruling in Cook's case earlier this year barred Trump from firing a Fed governor at will, noting the need for the Fed to remain politically independent, both in fact and in appearance, to do its job.

The Fed raised its policy rate in September and is expected to do so again at its final meeting of the year.
cd4883b44cbfd3ff: GENEVA: UN human rights experts on Tuesday slammed what they called the "severe crackdown" on LGBTQ organisations in Turkey, saying legitimate rights work was being unduly restricted.
Turkey's LGBTQ community has increasingly come under pressure from the authorities, with president Recep Tayyip Erdogan describing it as a "deviant movement" of "perverts".
The authorities recently launched a major clampdown on the LGBTQ community, raiding gay bars, nightclubs and the homes of activists and community members.

"Turkey must end the harassment of LGBTI human rights defenders and organisations and ensure a safe and enabling environment in which they can exercise their rights to freedom of expression, peaceful assembly and association and continue their legitimate work without fear of arrest, intimidation, stigmatisation or criminalisation," the UN experts said in a statement.
Although same-sex relations are legal in Turkey, hostility towards LGBTQ people remains widespread.
The UN experts said Turkey's justice ministry has announced judicial measures against more than 160 individuals and 20 associations and businesses.
On Sept 30, as part of its "My Family is Safe" operation, Turkey shut down the website and social media accounts of T24, a leading independent digital news website, citing its "LGBT propaganda".

"We are concerned that investigations reportedly invoke offences relating to 'obscenity', 'morality' and prostitution, alongside official statements describing associations as promoting 'LGBT and immorality' and the framing of LGBTI persons as a threat to families," the UN experts said.
"We demand an immediate end to the so-called 'My Family Is Safe' operation.
"We demand the immediate release of persons detained solely for their legitimate human rights work."
The experts included the special rapporteurs on human rights defenders, the independence of judges, freedom of expression, and freedom of peaceful association.
The statement was also penned by the expert on protection against violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity.
UN experts are independent figures appointed by the Human Rights Council. They do not, therefore, speak for the United Nations itself.
The experts said they were in contact with the Turkish government on the matter.

Turkish justice minister Akin Gurlek has said the "My Family is Safe" operation was launched as part of Erdogan's "Decade of the Family", which is aimed at "protecting our children, the institution of the family and social order".
413ddc4cc59ab03b: MALAYSIANS should not have to become fire investigators to ask for cleaner air.
When smoke crosses borders, frustration is understandable. People want those responsible held accountable and assurance that the same ordeal will not return.
The difficulty is that a satisfying explanation is not always a sufficient one.
Naming a company, blaming a farmer or condemning an entire industry may settle an argument in the comments section. It does considerably less to settle the embers.
After a working life spent largely in plantations, I believe the debate needs to begin with a practical test: will our response help prevent the next fire?
That means examining how land is managed, how quickly danger is detected and whether people have the resources to respond.
Responsibility matters throughout. But identifying a culprit and understanding why a landscape keeps burning are related tasks, not interchangeable ones.
Consider the smaller farmer for whom burning is an inexpensive way to clear land.
A prohibition does not put a machine in the field or make credit affordable. Enforcement needs to come with workable alternatives, equipment and support.
Poverty cannot excuse every harmful practice. Equally, expecting compliance without considering its cost leaves a predictable gap between policy and reality.
Nor should the inquiry end at oil palm. Forestry concessions, other agricultural holdings and community land form part of the wider landscape.

For growers, deliberately burning productive palms makes no commercial sense. Effective prevention requires cooperation across it, including better peat and water management, early warnings, prompt field checks and adequate firefighting capacity.
The people providing that capacity deserve attention too. Government crews, estate employees, villagers, smallholders and volunteers all have a part.
Their work continues after the pictures stop circulating: replenishing water, maintaining firebreaks, checking embers and returning to places thought to be safe.
Acknowledging their effort grants nobody immunity from investigation. It simply recognises that a landscape under scrutiny may also contain people working hard to protect it.
Satellite monitoring is invaluable in directing attention to possible fires. The difficulty comes when an alert is treated as a completed investigation.

Heat detected inside a concession establishes a reason to investigate that location. It does not, on its own, establish the ignition point, who was responsible or whether failures in prevention or response contributed to the damage.

A fire may have started within the holding, crossed from adjacent land or re-emerged from smouldering peat. These possibilities need field evidence, not a preference for whichever explanation suits one's position.

Operators have obligations here. Anyone attributing a fire to neighbouring land should substantiate the claim. Anyone promising effective prevention should demonstrate how those arrangements performed under pressure.
A well-written policy is useful; a functioning response is rather more useful when vegetation is burning.
Prolonged dry weather makes that response harder by increasing flammability and reducing available water.
Peat may continue burning beneath the surface, with renewed flames appearing later. Fewer satellite detections therefore warrant caution before declaring success.
Such conditions help explain the challenge. They do not remove responsibility for deliberate burning or negligent management.
There is another complication: some operators are easier to scrutinise because their boundaries and commitments are public.
Less visible actors may attract less attention simply because information about them is harder to obtain.
The answer is wider scrutiny, not leniency for certified businesses.
Certification sets commitments against which performance should be judged; it neither proves innocence nor makes every fire within a boundary proof of guilt.
Public claims deserve equal scrutiny. Percentages need context: what was counted, excluded and over which period?
Companies and campaigners alike can select figures that are mathematically accurate yet misleading.
Anyone making claims that affect reputations, purchasing or regulation should explain their evidence and give corrections due prominence when findings change.

For Malaysians breathing polluted air, careful investigation may seem frustratingly slow. Yet establishing responsibility accurately makes accountability stronger and corrective action more effective.
Examine operators and regulators. Hear communities. Test industry explanations and campaign allegations. Act firmly on proven wrongdoing and correct unsupported accusations.
Judge progress by better prevention, fair accountability and fewer people breathing the same smoke again.
Cleaner air depends on getting the response right, not merely winning the argument. Every fire season produces enough heat; our public debate should bring more light.

2a37b990a48de89b: WASHINGTON: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio will this week lead a large business delegation to Uzbekistan and join a ministerial meeting with five Central Asian nations, before traveling to India, the State Department said Tuesday.

Traveling between Oct 17 and 22, Rubio will first go to Samarkand, Uzbekistan, for a "C5+1 Ministerial" and bilateral meetings with Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.

"On this historic visit, Secretary Rubio will lead a US commercial delegation comprised of over 200 business leaders, ushering in a new era of strengthened commercial cooperation for the US and Central Asia," a State Department statement said.
US President Donald Trump hosted the leaders of the five resource-rich Central Asian nations at the White House last November.

Rubio will then make his second official visit of the year to India, spending Oct 17-22 in the cities of Mumbai and Jamnagar and meeting with senior government officials "to strengthen the US-India strategic partnership, exchange views on regional and global dynamics, and discuss prospects for enhanced energy cooperation."
He will also meet business leaders "to promote opportunities for commercial investment and economic cooperation," the statement said.
Rubio last visited India in May, traveling to four cities over four days in a country that successive US administrations saw as a like-minded partner in a world dominated by China's rise.
Trump has shaken up that approach, temporarily imposing high tariffs and warming to both China and India's historic adversary Pakistan.
e4b29de992cdf4c8: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia must turn European investments into a catalyst for technology transfer, skilled job creation and stronger local industries as it seeks to move up the global value chain amid intensifying US-China competition, economists said.
Achieving this will require more than attracting foreign capital, they said in response to Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani's remarks.

Johari said Malaysia wanted European investments to facilitate technology transfer, develop highly skilled talent and create better-paying jobs as the country moves into its next phase of economic development.

He said the emphasis was shifting towards the quality and long-term value of inbound investments, with the ultimate goal of moving beyond participation in global value chains to creating and capturing more value within them.

"Ultimately, our objective is to move beyond simply participating in global value chains to capturing and creating greater value within them," he said at European Union-Malaysia Business Day 2026: Selangor in Focus today.

Economists said stronger links between multinational companies and local suppliers, particularly small and medium enterprises (SMEs), alongside targeted investment incentives and skills development, will be crucial to ensuring domestic businesses capture more value from foreign investments.

EU-Asean Business Council executive director Chris Humphrey said Malaysia could build on its existing attractiveness as a foreign direct investment (FDI)destination to draw more European companies into the country.
The recent announcement of a significant investment in semiconductor production by Nasdaq-listed NXP Semiconductors NV underscored Malaysia's appeal to international investors, he said.
However, sustaining that appeal and attracting more high-value activities would also depend on improving market access and giving businesses greater certainty to invest for the long term.
Humphrey said the swift conclusion of a high-quality, deep and comprehensive Malaysia-European Union free trade agreement (FTA) would be an important step towards achieving this.
"We have seen a steep increase in EU investments in Vietnam since the EU-Vietnam FTA was implemented, and given Malaysia's economic fundamentals, I would expect a similar pattern to emerge," he said.
A comprehensive agreement could boost business confidence by opening up new sectors, removing trade barriers and providing greater certainty for companies on both sides, he added.

While an FTA could help attract more European capital, Universiti Teknologi Mara senior lecturer Dr Mohamad Idham Md Razak said Malaysia would need complementary domestic policies to ensure those investments strengthened local capabilities.

He said investment incentives should be tied to measurable outcomes, including the employment of skilled local workers, development of domestic suppliers, workforce training and collaboration with Malaysian universities and research institutions.
The government should also strengthen technical and vocational education and training to ensure local talent could fill higher-skilled positions.
"Ultimately, the objective is to move Malaysian companies beyond basic assembly and subcontracting into engineering, product design, advanced manufacturing and innovation," he told Business Times.
Idham said the proposed Malaysia-EU FTA could help attract higher-quality investments by improving market access, reducing trade barriers and providing greater regulatory predictability.
However, an agreement alone would not guarantee technology transfer or meaningful benefits for local businesses.

Its effectiveness would depend on complementary measures, including stronger intellectual property protection, more efficient customs procedures, clearer investment regulations and better access to financing for SMEs seeking to meet European standards.

He said the government should also facilitate partnerships between European investors and local suppliers through supplier-development programmes, industry-academia collaboration and targeted skills training.
With effective implementation, the agreement could help Malaysian businesses enter European markets, diversify export destinations and move into higher-value activities.

"The key measure of success should not simply be the volume of European investment attracted, but how much domestic capability, skilled employment and long-term economic value Malaysia gains from it," he said.
Nusantara Academy for Strategic Research senior fellow Dr Azmi Hassan said the push for higher-value investments reflected a broader shift in Malaysia's investment strategy over the past decade.

Previously, Malaysia focused on attracting FDI by highlighting its political stability, safe investment environment and availability of low-cost labour. That approach was no longer sufficient as the country sought to compete for more sophisticated investments, he said.

Malaysia was now targeting high-technology investments in areas such as artificial intelligence (AI) and the green economy, with greater emphasis on technology transfer and developing a highly skilled local workforce.
Rather than competing on low labour costs, Malaysia needed to offer skilled talent and the expertise required to support higher-value activities, he said.
The country was also strengthening its infrastructure, including through the development of data centres, to support AI-related businesses and other technology-intensive investments.
Azmi said the ongoing negotiations for the Malaysia-EU FTA could further strengthen the country's appeal to European investors, particularly those in advanced technology, green technology and AI.

The agreement could deepen investment ties with Europe and encourage more companies to establish high-value operations in Malaysia, supporting the country's ambition to move beyond attracting capital towards building stronger domestic capabilities, he said.

ba47842c537c3b21: PETALING JAYA: Prasarana Malaysia Bhd is stepping up efforts to improve Light Rail Transit (LRT) reliability through round-the-clock maintenance, closer supplier engagement and the introduction of 26 new train sets for the Kelana Jaya Line.
The measures aim to address technical problems affecting train operations and improve the passenger experience.
Prasarana acting president and group chief executive officer Dr Prodyut Dutt acknowledged that the Kelana Jaya line had faced greater reliability challenges this year.
From January to August, the line recorded one incident for every 749km travelled, compared with one incident for every 1,066km during the same period last year.
"There is no denying the fact that we are having more incidents this year than we had last year. On the Kelana Jaya line, that represents a deterioration of about 30 per cent," he said.
In contrast, the Ampang line and Monorail recorded performance improvements of 20 per cent and 80 per cent respectively.
Dutt said prioritising the Kelana Jaya line was crucial as it carried the highest passenger volume, at 290,000 people daily.
He said 90 per cent of disruptions on the line stemmed from rolling stock issues, with two-thirds triggered by the automated emergency braking safety system.

The system activates automatically when onboard tachometer sensors, which monitor train wheel speeds, detect discrepancies of more than five per cent. Cable wear and track vibrations can affect the sensors and contribute to these discrepancies.
Dutt said the issue was linked to the operating characteristics of the line's linear induction motor (LIM) system, which has been in service since 1998.

"The design characteristic of a LIM system is that the braking is naturally very hard. Overseas operators using the same system, such as in Vancouver, face the same issues with tachometers and emergency braking."

However, Dutt said converting or replacing the LIM system entirely was not feasible as doing so would require the replacement of the power supply, signalling, trackwork and civil infrastructure. Prasarana, therefore, had to work within the system's existing design parameters.

On the condition of the fleet, he said the Kelana Jaya line operated 74 trains across three generations, including 26 first-generation four-car train sets that had been in service for more than 17 years.

An assessment found that overhauling trains aged 15 years would cost almost 90 per cent of the price of a new unit. This prompted Prasarana to order 26 new train sets worth more than RM1 billion from Chinese manufacturer CRRC Corporation Ltd.
The first new trains are scheduled to arrive in March 2029, with two sets expected to be delivered each month thereafter.

While the new fleet is expected to support long-term improvements, Dutt said Prasarana was also implementing interim measures and engineering interventions to stabilise operations before the trains arrived.
"That is why we are aggressively implementing interim measures and engineering interventions to stabilise operations."
Prasarana has also worked with CRRC to refine the braking profile of the new trains during the final design review, aiming to ensure smoother deceleration and improve passenger comfort.
To ease the immediate strain, Prasarana has introduced round-the-clock maintenance operations across its depots and specialised workshops to inspect, service and repair train systems.
During a recent visit to its facilities, a first-hand look at the operations was provided, including intensive maintenance work in the electrical, door system and main repair workshops.

However, Dutt said global supply chain bottlenecks remained a challenge, with critical components such as tachometers facing lead times of eight to 12 months. This had prompted senior engineering teams to meet suppliers directly to expedite orders.
"Cost is not the issue because the government has been very supportive through government guarantees and approved five-year funding programmes. Our main challenge is the lead time for spare parts."

He added that a major overhaul of the train bogies - the heavy undercarriage structures housing the wheels, suspension and braking systems - on the nine-year-old third-generation trains was scheduled to begin in June or July next year.

To minimise the impact of service disruptions on passengers, Prasarana is refining its contingency measures. These include turning trains back at selected locations to reduce congestion at key stations, isolating affected track sections, operating shuttle services and deploying feeder buses.
Dutt said passenger communication was also being strengthened through one-way WhatsApp broadcast alerts for registered users.
The presence of auxiliary police, station officers and Prasarana Troopers is also being increased on station platforms and in concourses to help manage passenger flow. Bernama

639a50988ea43d41: PETALING JAYA: A minimum starting salary of RM2,500 for graduates will do little to raise wages even as it seeks to address a longstanding structural weakness in Malaysia’s labour market, economists say.

Geoffrey Williams of Williams Business Consultancy Sdn Bhd pointed out that graduates already earn between RM2,500 and RM3,500 a month, while Yeah Kim Leng of Sunway University said the proposed rate was “reasonable as a legal floor” but still fell short of a living wage in major cities.

On the other hand, Barjoyai Bardai of the Malaysia University of Science and Technology said the proposal was pertinent given that academic qualifications and skills did not always translate into adequate remuneration.
Under Budget 2027, tabled by Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim last Friday, the government proposed a starting salary of at least RM2,500 a month for graduates and semi-skilled workers.

Anwar, who is also finance minister, said the move would ensure that pay scales reflected workers’ academic qualifications rather than being based solely on the general national minimum wage, which has been raised from RM1,700 to RM2,000.
Williams said graduates’ starting salaries were determined by market conditions, adding that employers could choose not to hire graduates at any wage level.
He said setting a minimum starting salary could also result in some graduates’ employment contracts not being renewed.
“So this (RM2,500 minimum salary) is a double-edged sword. It looks like a sharp policy to help graduates, but it also cuts their employability.”
Yeah said that while a RM2,500 minimum starting salary was “reasonable as a legal floor”, it fell short of a living wage in major cities.

Citing official data, he said single individuals in Kuala Lumpur needed RM2,403 a month to maintain a decent standard of living, while those in Klang needed RM2,161. The corresponding figure for those in Penang’s Timur Laut district was RM2,180.

Yeah said the minimum starting salary should be determined through a tripartite negotiation mechanism involving the government, employers and workers, rather than being dictated solely by market forces or rigidly fixed by the government. Neither extreme, he said, would be suitable for Malaysia’s circumstances.

He said market forces had already suppressed graduate wages, with 65% earning below RM3,000 a month. He added that inflation-adjusted median entry-level salaries for bachelor’s degree holders had fallen by 10% over 25 years.
A blanket national rate for graduates and semi-skilled workers, he said, would overlook significant regional differences in living costs and could have unintended negative consequences.
“The RM2,500 figure is defensible as a starting benchmark, but the actual rate should be calibrated to what employers can sustainably pay in different regions.”

Barjoyai said a monthly salary of RM2,500 or more could also help improve young workers’ purchasing power, particularly for those who needed to cover accommodation, transport, food, education loan repayments and other living expenses.
“It could also help narrow the gap between the cost of acquiring qualifications and the financial returns graduates receive upon entering employment,” he said when contacted.
However, Barjoyai cautioned against treating the RM2,500 figure “as an end in itself”, given the government’s aim of transitioning to a high-productivity, high-income economy.
“The RM2,500 starting salary can be one instrument towards that objective, provided it is accompanied by effective skills development, technological adoption and stronger demand for skilled labour.”
He warned that setting a minimum salary without considering differences in productivity, industry conditions and employers’ ability to pay could have unintended consequences.
These included reduced recruitment, delayed business expansion and a shift towards contractual arrangements that lower employment costs.
39737f2ba49f8f3a: PETALING JAYA: For nearly two decades, Malaysian Dogs Deserve Better (MDDB) has rescued and cared for strays that had nowhere else to go. Now, the organisation itself is struggling to survive.
With nearly 400 dogs under its care and high monthly expenses, dwindling donations and rising veterinary costs have left its future uncertain.
Among those most vulnerable are its elderly, disabled and terminally ill dogs, many of which depend on regular medication and frequent veterinary treatment.
“We need RM60,000 a month, including veterinary bills, because we provide palliative care,” said founding member Irene Low, 61.
“We have many elderly and disabled dogs, as well as those with kidney and liver problems. Two of our dogs also have mental health issues. They require long-term medication and daily vet visits.”

While veterinary bills account for the largest share of MDDB’s expenses, the organisation must also cover workers’ wages, utilities and rent for a bungalow housing dogs that need more specialised care.
Its main shelter in Rawang, where its able-bodied dogs live, is rent-free.
Yet regular donations are no longer enough to meet those costs. Members have been making up the shortfall from their own pockets, but they can no longer afford to do so indefinitely.
Low said some long-time donors have died or retired, while others had to stop contributing after closing their businesses, particularly in the years following 2020.
“When we started out 18 years ago, more people could seemingly afford to sponsor our dogs. Some would sponsor 15 or 20 dogs and pay for the entire year,” she recalled.
At the same time, many of the dogs MDDB rescued in its early years are themselves growing old, bringing greater medical needs and higher veterinary bills.
The organisation’s ageing founders, meanwhile, have had to navigate a changing landscape of animal welfare and fundraising.
Financial pressures have also forced MDDB to scale back one of the most expensive parts of its rescue work: helping dogs injured in accidents.
“We can no longer rescue as many accident victims as we used to because taking an injured dog to the vet and paying for its treatment can be very expensive,” Low said.
MDDB is now seeking businesses and individuals willing to provide regular financial assistance for at least a year.
“If we receive support for a whole year, we can plan our next move instead of constantly worrying about how to raise enough money to pay our bills each month,” she explained.

Additionally, the public can help through MDDB’s sponsorship programme, which costs RM100 a month for an able-bodied dog and RM150 for a disabled animal. The organisation also welcomes donations in kind and assistance with fundraising events.
“We need support urgently,” Low stressed.
For the hundreds of dogs that have come to know MDDB as home, that support could mean the difference between uncertainty and the chance to remain somewhere they are safe, cared for and loved.
Those who wish to contribute can donate to MDDB Canine Welfare Society, Public Bank account 3237 688 227.
