2ae1c6a00e65c083: PETALING JAYA: Gaji permulaan minimum RM2,500 bagi graduan tidak akan membawa banyak perubahan dalam meningkatkan kadar upah walaupun bertujuan menangani kelemahan struktur sudah lama berakar dalam pasaran buruh, kata ahli ekonomi.

Geoffrey Williams daripada Williams Business Consultancy Sdn Bhd berkata, graduan ketika ini sudah pun meraih pendapatan antara RM2,500 hingga RM3,500 sebulan, manakala Yeah Kim Leng daripada Sunway University berkata, kadar dicadangkan itu 'munasabah menjadi dasar undang-undang', namun masih belum mencapai paras gaji kehidupan wajar di bandar utama.

Dalam pada itu, Barjoyai Bardai daripada Universiti Sains dan Teknologi Malaysia berkata, cadangan berkenaan tepat memandangkan kelayakan akademik dan kemahiran tidak sentiasa diterjemahkan kepada imbuhan sewajarnya.
Dalam Belanjawan 2027 dibentangkan Perdana Menteri, Anwar Ibrahim, Jumaat lalu, kerajaan mencadangkan gaji permulaan sekurang-kurangnya RM2,500 sebulan bagi graduan dan pekerja separa mahir.

Anwar yang juga menteri kewangan berkata, langkah itu akan memastikan tangga gaji mencerminkan kelayakan akademik pekerja dan bukan berasaskan kadar gaji minimum kebangsaan semata-mata, yang naik daripada RM1,700 kepada RM2,000.
Williams berkata, gaji permulaan graduan ditentukan oleh keadaan pasaran, sambil menambah majikan boleh memilih untuk tidak mengambil graduan bekerja pada mana-mana paras gaji.
Katanya, menetapkan gaji permulaan minimum juga boleh mengakibatkan sesetengah kontrak pekerjaan graduan tidak diperbaharui.
“Jadi, (gaji minimum RM2,500) jadi 'pedang bermata dua'. Ia nampak macam dasar tegas membantu graduan, tetapi turut mengekang kebolehpasaran mereka," katanya.
Yeah berkata, walaupun gaji permulaan RM2,500 'munasabah menjadi dasar undang-undang', ia masih belum mencapai paras gaji wajar di bandar utama.

Memetik data rasmi, beliau berkata individu bujang di Kuala Lumpur memerlukan RM2,403 sebulan untuk mengekalkan taraf hidup selesa, manakala mereka di Klang memerlukan RM2,161. Angka sepadan bagi mereka di daerah Timur Laut, Pulau Pinang pula RM2,180.

Katanya, gaji permulaan minimum sepatutnya ditentukan menerusi mekanisme perundingan tiga pihak melibatkan kerajaan, majikan, dan pekerja, berbanding ditetapkan sepenuhnya oleh kuasa pasaran atau dilaraskan secara tegar oleh kerajaan.
Beliau berkata, dua 'pendekatan melampau' itu tidak sesuai dengan keadaan di Malaysia.
Katanya, kuasa pasaran semasa sudah menekan gaji graduan dengan 65% daripada mereka meraih pendapatan bawah RM3,000 sebulan.
Menurutnya, gaji penanda aras kemasukan pertengahan yang dilaraskan mengikut inflasi bagi pemegang ijazah sarjana muda telah menurun 10% dalam tempoh 25 tahun.

Yeah berkata, satu kadar kebangsaan menyeluruh bagi graduan dan pekerja separa mahir akan mengabaikan perbezaan kos sara hidup yang ketara mengikut wilayah, dan boleh membawa kesan negatif yang bukan disengajakan.
“Angka RM2,500 itu boleh dipertahankan sebagai penanda aras permulaan, tetapi kadar sebenar sepatutnya dilaraskan mengikut keupayaan pembayaran majikan secara mampan di pelbagai wilayah berbeza.”

Barjoyai berkata, gaji RM2,500 atau lebih berupaya membantu meningkatkan kuasa beli pekerja muda, terutama bagi mereka yang perlu menampung kos penginapan, pengangkutan, makanan, bayaran balik pinjaman pendidikan, dan perbelanjaan sara hidup lain.
“Ia juga dapat membantu merapatkan jurang antara kos untuk memperoleh kelayakan akademik dengan pulangan kewangan diterima graduan apabila mula melangkah ke alam pekerjaan,” katanya.

Bagaimanapun, beliau mengingatkan agar jumlah RM2,500 itu tidak dijadikan 'matlamat akhir semata-mata', memandangkan hasrat kerajaan untuk beralih kepada ekonomi berproduktivi dan berpendapatan tinggi.

“Gaji permulaan RM2,500 ini boleh menjadi instrumen ke arah objektif berkenaan dengan syarat disertai pembangunan kemahiran yang berkesan, penerapan teknologi, dan permintaan lebih kukuh terhadap tenaga kerja mahir," katanya.
Beliau memberi amaran menetapkan gaji minimum tanpa mengambil kira perbezaan dalam produktiviti, keadaan industri, dan keupayaan majikan membayar juga membawa kesan lain.
Ia termasuk pengurangan pengambilan pekerja, penangguhan perluasan perniagaan, dan peralihan ke arah pengaturan secara kontrak bagi mengurangkan kos pekerjaan.
ba3592d742f234cb: KUALA LUMPUR: Aaron Chia-Soh Wooi Yik made a winning return as a permanent partnership, defeating defending champions Takuro Hoki-Yugo Kobayashi of Japan in the Denmark Open first round in Odense on Tuesday.

The world No. 4 Malaysians, playing together for the first time since their World Championships silver medal feat in August, battled for 51 minutes before prevailing 21-19, 14-21, 21-11 in a clash between two former world champion pairs.

The victory was a fitting start to their renewed partnership, which has been given the green light to continue until the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics following a brief separation under national men's doubles coach Herry Iman Pierngadi's reshuffling exercise.
For Wooi Yik, reuniting with Aaron after a decade together carries special significance, particularly with their Olympic gold dream still unfulfilled.
"It's special to be back again. I think we've been partners for 10 years," said Wooi Yik in a post-match interview.
"I think we both have our own dream that we haven't achieved yet. We still have something to push for.
"My focus, obviously, is LA. We hope that we can show more maturity and experience in our gameplay."
The pair, who won Olympic bronze medals at Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024, had requested to resume their partnership following their silver medal at the World Championships in New Delhi.
Their wishes were eventually granted after discussions involving BA of Malaysia (BAM) performance committee chairman Datuk Seri Lee Chong Wei and the national coaching team.
During their temporary separation, Aaron partnered youngster Aaron Tai and reached the Taiwan Open final, while Wooi Yik finished runner-up at the Korea Masters alongside Man Wei Chong.
Aaron acknowledged that playing with scratch partners carried different expectations compared with an established combination.
He felt the temporary partnerships sometimes allowed players to perform more freely without the pressure associated with a long-standing pairing.
Nonetheless, the 29-year-old believes their preparations for Los Angeles remain on course.
"I think we're on track," said Aaron, who added that their focus would be on building towards 2027.
Their reunion could hardly have begun against tougher opponents.
Hoki-Kobayashi, the 2021 world champions and world No. 8, held a commanding advantage in their previous meetings, although the Malaysians had beaten them at last year's Singapore Open.
Tuesday's victory extended Aaron-Wooi Yik's winning streak against the Japanese to two matches despite trailing 9-4 in their overall head-to-head record.
Aaron credited their improved concentration and fewer unforced errors in the deciding game for the victory.
"We focused on what we had to do in the third game and grabbed our opportunities," he said.
"We've played them many times, so we know each other's game. We just had to focus and make fewer unforced errors."
The fourth seeds, who won the Denmark Open in 2023, will face either South Korea's Kang Min Hyuk-Lee Jong Min or compatriots Aaron Tai-Yap Roy King in the second round.
An all-Malaysian clash would provide another interesting subplot, with Aaron Tai-Roy King arriving in Denmark fresh from winning the Arctic Open title in Finland on Sunday.
Meanwhile, K. Letshanaa's struggles continued as the world No. 27 suffered a 21-5, 21-18 defeat to home favourite and world No. 12 Line Christophersen in just 32 minutes.
It was Letshanaa's second defeat in as many meetings against the Dane, following their German Open encounter last year.

The latest setback extended a worrying run for the 23-year-old, who has failed to progress beyond the second round in eight consecutive individual tournaments since reaching the Malaysia Masters quarter-finals in May.
Five of those campaigns ended in the opening round, raising concerns over her ability to maintain the top-30 ranking she worked hard to achieve.

It represents a sharp contrast to her promising start to 2026, when she reached the Indonesia Masters semi-finals and the quarter-finals of both the Thailand Masters and Malaysia Masters, the latter featuring a breakthrough victory over Japan's then-world No. 9 Tomoka Miyazaki.

21c8671a75203ee4: SANAA: Saudi Arabia said on Wednesday that an attack on an Aramco building in the kingdom's east sparked a "limited fire", while debris from intercepted Houthi missiles wounded four people in the capital, Riyadh.
It came hours after the Saudi-led coalition battling Yemen's Houthis said it had intercepted several missiles on Tuesday evening, including over Riyadh.

A Saudi energy ministry official said an administrative building belonging to oil giant Aramco in Dhahran was struck on Tuesday evening, resulting in a "limited fire" but "no casualties or fatalities".

Saudi Arabia's civil defence agency said on Wednesday that four people — two women, a man and a child — were wounded by debris from two intercepted Houthi cruise missiles in the capital, and that 15 homes were damaged.
Earlier on Tuesday, the coalition struck oil sites across western Yemen in response to the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in years.

The strikes in Yemen's Sanaa and the western provinces of Dhamar and Saada targeted facilities used to "supply the war effort" by the Houthis to "threaten the kingdom, Yemen, the southern Red Sea and waterways", coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki wrote on X.
A powerful explosion then rang out in the Saudi capital, with a phone alert sent to residents saying "the city of Riyadh is facing a hostile aerial threat".

While walking down a major avenue in Riyadh, a witness told AFP he "saw a projectile cutting across the sky" above a mall, saying it left "a yellowish trail of light followed by a trail of smoke. Then, we heard an explosion".
"People were calm; no one was speaking. We were scared and all looking up at the sky," he added, requesting anonymity.

After Houthi strikes on Saudi airports and energy sites in recent days, the coalition issued its first evacuation order in the Yemeni capital since the war flared in July, before attacking the Yemen Petroleum Company facility on Sanaa's outskirts.
An AFP correspondent in Sanaa reported an explosion, while a breaking news alert on the Houthi-affiliated Al-Masirah TV channel said "Saudi aggression" had targeted the oil firm.
Renewed threats
A strike on Riyadh's international airport on Saturday left 13 people dead and operations suspended in the worst attack since 2015.

The Saudi cabinet vowed at a meeting earlier on Tuesday, led by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, that it "will not allow its security or freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab Strait to be threatened".
An AFP correspondent reported that many civilians in Sanaa, fearing shortages, rushed to queue in front of fuel stations after the coalition warning.
The Houthis had earlier issued a new threat to target Riyadh's international airport, a refinery and an Aramco facility in Dammam if the strike went ahead, calling on citizens to avoid them.
Many countries have issued travel warnings to their citizens in Saudi Arabia. Most recently, France told its citizens to avoid Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam airports.
The Saudi-led coalition has supported Yemen's government militarily against the Houthis since 2015 in a long-running civil war that has created a dire humanitarian crisis.
Economic woes
Traffic in perennially gridlocked Riyadh was noticeably lighter this week as remote learning for all schools and work-from-home orders for some companies took effect, according to AFP journalists.

Saudi Arabia faces a major economic contraction this year, with GDP expected to shrink 3.3 per cent, the International Monetary Fund said on Tuesday, predicting a regional downturn due to Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.
The kingdom was already facing headwinds from Iran's chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz since the start of the Middle East war in February, when the US and Israel attacked Iran.
But the resumption in July of Yemen's frozen war has further roiled the kingdom and brought the fighting to its own soil.
Houthi attacks have also targeted oil tankers in the Red Sea — Saudi Arabia's alternative export route.
In Yemen, the renewed fighting was fuelling the risk of infectious disease outbreaks.
Suspected cholera cases tripled there in three weeks, the World Health Organisation said on Tuesday, warning that the growing disease burden was straining hospitals already treating war casualties.
'Behaving very badly'
The Riyadh airport attack had prompted US President Donald Trump to say he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis.
He wrote on his Truth Social platform on Tuesday that "the Houthis are behaving very badly", accusing them of acting "probably at the behest of Iran".
"I'll be there after the elections, and I will never forget!" he wrote, referring to next month's midterm elections.
The Houthis warned the US against intervention, with political bureau member Mohammed Al Bukhaiti telling AFP they would target American interests in the region.
Bukhaiti said the purpose of the campaign against Saudi targets was to send a message to the crown prince "that he can no longer wage aggression against Yemen from a safe position".

ca4384d768c0c039: MOSCOW: Russia's FSB security agency said on Tuesday it had detained a Japanese journalist for alleged espionage, and Moscow's foreign ministry said it regretted that Tokyo was using correspondents to carry out spying.

In a statement on its website, the FSB said the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper journalist was detained in the far eastern Sakhalin region on the day before he planned to leave Russia. It did not specify when this was.

Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova in a statement identified the journalist as Imai Yuki, according to the Russian transliteration of his name, and said his detention cast a new pall on relations with Tokyo.
Japan's embassy in Moscow did not answer phone calls outside of business hours.
In a Russian state TV video report on the case, three masked men in black uniforms handcuffed a man lying on the ground as a voice off camera said he was suspected of spying.

The agency "thwarted the illegal activity" of the journalist, the FSB said.

"As a result of intelligence operations, it was established that he gathered and stored information related to the country's defence capabilities in order to pass it on for national intelligence purposes to be used against the security of the Russian Federation," the statement said.

The foreign ministry spokeswoman said, "Tokyo's attempts to use its correspondents in Russia with the status of foreign journalists to gather information for undermining our state's security are regrettable."
Japan, she said, had adopted an anti-Russian position during Russia's military campaign in Ukraine and refused to consider Moscow's concerns about Tokyo's "remilitarisation".
"We have to note that what has occurred will become an additional factor clouding the atmosphere of Russian-Japanese relations," Zakharova said.
Russia regards Japan as an "unfriendly" country because it has joined Western sanctions against Moscow over the war in Ukraine.
Russia and Japan, which never signed a formal World War Two peace treaty, have a territorial dispute over the Kuril Islands, known in Japan as the Northern Territories.

Russian president Vladimir Putin visited one of the disputed islands in August, causing an uproar in Japan. Tokyo has said it would continue implementing sanctions against Russia and supporting Ukraine.
One of the most prominent cases of a foreign journalist arrested in Russia was the detention of Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich in 2023.

13096602de9f3aae: From Boo Jia Cher
The chaos at Sepang International Circuit during the Formula 1 weekend was frustrating, but hardly surprising.

Thousands of fans were left stranded. Crowds spilled onto the highway, with some fans walking along emergency lanes towards Kuala Lumpur International Airport. Shuttle buses struggled to cope with the sudden surge, while traffic around the circuit ground to a standstill.
It would be easy to dismiss this as a one-off failure of event management. But for anyone who uses Malaysian public transport every day, the problems at Sepang should look very familiar.
Sepang was simply a much bigger, more visible version of the transport problems we already face in our cities.
We still don't take buses seriously
At the heart of the problem is a basic mistake in how we design our roads: buses are still treated as a mode of transport that has to squeeze into traffic, rather than being given priority.
Whenever a major event is expected to attract large crowds, the usual solution is simple: add more buses.

However, putting more buses onto the same congested roads does not solve much. A bus is only useful if it can actually move. A 12-metre bus carrying 50 or 60 people has little advantage over dozens of cars if it is stuck in the same traffic.
That is what happened at Sepang. Once the roads around the circuit became jammed, the shuttle buses could not bypass the congestion. They became part of it.

If a bus that normally takes 20 minutes to complete a trip takes two hours instead, the number of passengers it can carry over the course of the day collapses. Adding more buses only helps if there is enough road capacity for them to move.

This is the same problem commuters face every morning on roads such as Jalan Ampang and the Federal Highway. You can see buses sitting in the same three-lane traffic jam as everyone else while carrying dozens of passengers who chose public transport to avoid sitting in traffic.

A bus carrying 50 people should not have to compete for road space with 50 separate cars. If we want buses to work, they need dedicated, physically protected bus lanes that cannot simply become another lane for cars whenever traffic gets bad.
Grab is not mass transit

Another problem is the tendency to lump taxis and e-hailing services such as Grab into the same category as public transport. They are useful, of course. But they are not a substitute for mass transit.

A Grab car still occupies roughly the same road space as any other car. And when tens of thousands of people leave an event at roughly the same time, asking each person to book an individual car creates an enormous amount of traffic.
Cars have to queue to pick people up, stop at roadsides, make U-turns and squeeze through already crowded roads.

One bus can carry dozens of people in a single vehicle. To move the same number of passengers using individual cars requires a long line of vehicles. That difference matters enormously when road space is limited.

Instead of using e-hailing as a substitute for public transport, planners should treat it as a feeder service that helps people get to rail stations and bus hubs, rather than something that replaces high-capacity transport altogether. Otherwise, we end up filling our roads with hundreds of low-capacity vehicles precisely when we need to move the most people.
The problem doesn't stop at Sepang
There is another problem that is easier to miss. Where do all those extra buses and drivers come from?

In an already underserved public transport system, buses and drivers have to be pulled from regular routes to serve major events. That means someone elsewhere can end up waiting longer for a bus simply because another part of the country is hosting a major event.

This is a sign of how little spare capacity our bus networks have. A healthy public transport system should have enough buses and drivers to handle a major event without effectively robbing one to pay another.
A weekend transport surge can put pressure on ordinary commuters in surrounding neighbourhoods. People who had nothing to do with the event can end up paying for it through longer waiting times.
Johor Bahru should take note

Sepang should also be a warning for Johor Bahru. The upcoming RTS Link will bring large numbers of passengers directly into Bukit Chagar and central Johor Bahru. The rail connection itself is a major and potentially transformative investment.
However, trains do not exist in isolation. What happens after passengers leave the station matters just as much.

If thousands of commuters step out from the Bukit Chagar station and find themselves surrounded by cars, taxis and e-hailing vehicles fighting for space on already congested roads, we could end up recreating the same problem as Sepang, but every day.

Johor Bahru also has a basic problem with walkability. Walking between Bukit Chagar and nearby parts of the city can still mean dealing with broken pavements, a lack of shade, missing crossings and wide, intimidating roads.

A person should not need a car just to cross the street or walk a few hundred metres from a train station. If walking is unpleasant and buses are stuck in traffic, many people will simply choose to drive or book a Grab instead. That adds even more cars to the streets around the station.

The RTS can bring huge numbers of people into the city, but the city still needs to give those people somewhere to go. That means proper pedestrian connections, safe crossings, shaded walkways and dedicated bus lanes should be treated as part of the RTS investment, not as optional improvements to be dealt with later.
We cannot traffic-manage our way out of this

The response to the Sepang chaos focused heavily on traffic police, lane diversions and managing the flow of vehicles. Those things have their place, but they cannot solve a more fundamental problem: too many people are being asked to use the same limited road space at the same time.

We need to start designing our roads around how many people they can move, rather than how many cars they can accommodate. That means giving buses and other high-capacity vehicles priority on dedicated lanes.

It means managing e-hailing pick-up points so they do not clog the entrances to major transport hubs. Major events should also have enough dedicated transport capacity without stripping ordinary neighbourhood bus routes, while walking and cycling should be made a realistic part of the journey, especially around major train stations.

For one weekend, Sepang gave us an unusually clear view of a problem that normally plays out more quietly across Malaysian cities: we built our roads around cars, then expected public transport to somehow work within them.
The lesson from Sepang will keep repeating itself on our highways, outside our train stations, and on the daily commute home, as long as we don't fundamentally change our transport planning.
Boo Jia Cher is an FMT reader.

875f461cebb88877: PETALING JAYA: Kapal tempur pesisir (LCS) yang dijangka beroperasi sepenuhnya pada 2035 tidak semestinya usang jika sistem dan teknologinya terus dinaik taraf mengikut perkembangan ancaman ketenteraan, kata penganalisis pertahanan.
Zaki Salleh berkata, walaupun sebahagian sistem asal mungkin kurang relevan menjelang tempoh itu, keadaan tersebut tidak bermakna kapal berkenaan hilang nilai operasinya.
“Ya, ada kemungkinan sebahagian sistem asal tidak lagi berada pada tahap paling relevan ketika itu (2035), namun ini tidak bermakna LCS akan menjadi usang secara automatik,” katanya kepada FMT.

Pada 7 Okt lalu, Ahli Parlimen Kampar Chong Zemin mempersoalkan sama ada LCS Tentera Laut Diraja Malaysia (TLDM) masih mampu memenuhi keperluan pertahanan apabila mencapai keupayaan operasi penuh, kira-kira 24 tahun selepas projek itu diluluskan pada 2011.
Ia susulan Laporan Ketua Audit Negara (LKAN) 2/2026 dikeluarkan 5 Okt lalu mendapati kapal pertama, LCS 1 mungkin hanya dapat beroperasi sepenuhnya pada Disember 2035.

Zaki berkata, kapal perang moden lazimnya mempunyai hayat perkhidmatan antara 30 hingga 50 tahun, dengan sistem radar, komunikasi, persenjataan dan peperangan elektronik boleh diganti atau dinaik taraf.
Katanya, LCS perlu dilengkapi sistem radar, sensor dan pengurusan tempur yang mampu mengikuti perkembangan ancaman, termasuk serangan dron.
“Kapal itu juga perlu dihubungkan dengan rangkaian pertahanan bagi membolehkan perkongsian maklumat dengan kapal TLDM lain, pesawat Tentera Udara Diraja Malaysia (TUDM) dan dron,” katanya.

Bagaimanapun, Felo Kanan Global Peace Institute, Mizan Aslam, berkata kelewatan projek itu meningkatkan risiko teknologi LCS ketinggalan berikutan perkembangan pesat teknologi ketenteraan termasuk kecerdasan buatan (AI).
“Perubahan daripada sudut teknologi maklumat dan komunikasi, kemudian pergi kepada AI dan Revolusi Perindustrian 5.0, menjadikan perubahan sangat ketara dan cepat,” katanya.
Mizan turut mempersoalkan kemampuan LCS menampung teknologi dan persenjataan baharu, termasuk kapasiti membawa peluru berpandu yang menurutnya terhad kepada kira-kira 16 unit pada satu-satu masa.

Zaki berkata, selain isu teknologi, kelewatan projek menyebabkan TLDM perlu bergantung lebih lama pada kapal sedia ada, sekali gus menambah tekanan terhadap operasi, penyelenggaraan dan sumber manusia.
Mizan pula memberi amaran kekurangan aset boleh menjejaskan keupayaan Malaysia mempertahankan perairannya sebagai sebuah negara maritim.

Bagi mengisi jurang keupayaan sementara menunggu LCS mencapai kemampuan penuh, Zaki mencadangkan kerajaan mempercepat perolehan kapal misi pesisir (LMS) batch 3 yang dimasukkan dalam Rancangan Malaysia Ke-13.
Katanya, sekurang-kurangnya tiga kapal LMS perlu diperoleh, dengan jumlah itu boleh ditingkatkan kepada lima jika kemampuan kewangan mengizinkan.
“Memang LMS tidak menggantikan sepenuhnya keupayaan LCS, tetapi penambahan kapal mampu memberikan fleksibiliti operasi kepada TLDM,” katanya.
Beliau turut menggesa TLDM memperkemas penyelenggaraan dan naik taraf kapal sedia ada serta memperkukuh keupayaan perisikan, pengawasan dan peninjauan maritim.
Mizan pula mencadangkan kerajaan menilai semula kaedah perolehan aset pertahanan, termasuk mempertimbangkan pembelian kapal siap daripada pengeluar bagi mengurangkan risiko kelewatan.
b98d30e3400fd1e0: PETALING JAYA: The artery has been reopened. The procedure went well, follow-up results are reassuring, and the cardiologist says recovery is on track.

Yet the staircase that once required no thought can suddenly feel like a decision. A flight overseas, a return to exercise, or even an unfamiliar ache in the chest may raise the same unsettling question: what if it happens again?
For many heart-attack survivors, recovery does not end when the immediate danger has passed.

In 2020 and 2021, Malaysia recorded over 15,000 admissions for acute coronary syndrome, which includes heart attacks, according to the National Cardiovascular Disease Database. Behind those numbers are patients who must gradually learn to trust their bodies again.
Consultant cardiologist Dr Yew Kuan Leong said this process begins well before a person goes home.

“Recovery actually begins before the patient leaves the hospital,” he said. “It is not just about the angioplasty or stent procedure being successful, but also about what the patient does afterwards.”

That may involve medication, changes to diet and exercise, and cardiac rehabilitation where appropriate. How quickly someone returns to work, driving, travel and physical activity varies according to their condition and recovery.

But physical progress does not necessarily mean confidence returns at the same pace. Consultant cardiologist Dr Shathiskumar Govindaraju said a heart attack can leave some survivors fearful, irritable, low in mood or unable to sleep properly.

“A heart attack is not only a physical event, it can also be an emotional shock similar to a traumatic event,” he said. Some become acutely aware of every heartbeat or bodily sensation, while others worry constantly about another attack.
“Whenever I see a patient after a heart attack, I don’t just ask, ‘How is your chest?’ I also want to know, ‘How are you sleeping? How are you feeling? Are you afraid?’” Shathiskumar added.

That anxiety can make ordinary sensations suddenly seem ominous. Yew said some patients become worried by chest discomfort, headaches or numbness in a hand, fearing that each symptom signals another heart attack.
Not every sensation is heart-related, but patients should not attempt to diagnose themselves, either. New or worsening chest pain, breathlessness or fainting should always be medically assessed.
The doctors noted that some caution after a heart attack is useful. It can encourage people to take medication consistently, attend follow-ups and pay closer attention to their health.
The problem, Shathiskumar pointed out, lies in "whether fear is helping the patient protect their heart, or preventing them from living their life".

That may show up as repeatedly checking one’s pulse, constantly seeking reassurance or avoiding exercise, travel and social activities despite being medically cleared. Some patients may also become frightened of being alone.
Family members can help by taking those fears seriously rather than brushing them aside, while still encouraging the patient to follow medical advice and gradually resume everyday activities.

If anxiety, low mood or disturbed sleep persists for several weeks or starts interfering with normal life, patients should speak to a doctor. Persistent hopelessness, panic or thoughts of self-harm require prompt professional attention.

For those who have been cleared to become active again but remain hesitant, Yew recommends patience rather than either extreme. “Do not be afraid, but do be patient and take things one step at a time," he said.
Cardiac rehabilitation can be particularly useful because it provides a structured way to exercise, understand risk factors and regain confidence in what the body is capable of doing.
The good highway
There is also another misconception doctors frequently encounter: that once a blocked artery has been treated, the underlying heart disease has disappeared. It has not.
“I would describe angioplasty as creating a good ‘highway’ for the coronary artery, but the patient still has an important role in looking after that highway,” Yew said.

Angioplasty treats a blockage, but coronary artery disease can continue to progress. Medication, physical activity, healthier eating, not smoking and regular follow-up therefore remain important long after the procedure itself.
Treatment has also become more sophisticated as cardiologists increasingly encounter younger patients, more women, and complex disease involving multiple or heavily calcified arteries.
Newer imaging tools allow doctors to examine arteries more closely, while specialised techniques can help manage blockages that are more difficult to treat.
Even so, Shathiskumar said the measure of a successful recovery should extend beyond whether an artery has been reopened or a patient has survived the immediate event.
“We want them eventually to say, ‘I survived it, I recovered, and I’m living my life again.’”
468f3bfda6253d9e: PARIS: Atletico Madrid beat Manchester United 2-0 in the UEFA Champions League on Tuesday as the Red Devils continued their poor run, while Bayern Munich were held 3-3 in Norway by underdogs Viking Stavanger.
Elsewhere, last season's beaten finalists Arsenal eased to victory over Lille while Barcelona came from behind to beat Galatasaray but Inter Milan lost a seven-goal thriller at home to Club Brugge.

Atletico, who lost at Liverpool in their opening European encounter, took the lead inside the opening minute in the Spanish capital through Pablo Barrios. Alejandro Grimaldo struck the woodwork from a free-kick later in the first half.
Johnny Cardoso also had a goal disallowed before the break but Ademola Lookman got Atletico's second in the 79th minute, just after United defender Leny Yoro had been sent off.
The defeat continued the Old Trafford club's disappointing start to the campaign and increased the pressure on manager Michael Carrick.
They have gone five matches without a victory and have won only once in seven outings, with a trip to Italy to face Como next up in the Champions League.
"Tonight is a one-off game in judgement, it is the Champions League and a tough place to come. We are doing certain things OK," Carrick told broadcaster Amazon Prime.
Viking, who are in the Champions League after winning a first Norwegian title in 34 years, appeared to be heading for a famous win over Bayern when they led 2-0 at half-time in Stavanger.
Gianni Stensness headed them in front in the second minute and Peter Christiansen ran away to double their advantage.
Olise sent off
Harry Kane pulled one back from a penalty early in the second half and then headed in his eighth goal of the season in nine games in all competitions.

Luis Diaz then converted as the match was turned completely on its head, but Bayern's Michael Olise was sent off in the 74th minute -- the France star was booked and then shown a second yellow seconds later for throwing the ball at his opponent.
He will therefore miss next week's home meeting with Arsenal.
Viking snatched a memorable draw as Herman Haugen headed home in the last minute.

Speaking to Amazon Prime, Kane said Olise "will be gutted and he has to take responsibility for it. It was a mistake, and mistakes happen. He has to learn from it. It's a shame because we have important games ahead of us."

Arsenal were too strong for Lille as the Premier League champions won 3-0 at the Emirates Stadium with goals by Jurrien Timber, Eberechi Eze and Bukayo Saka, in the space of eight second-half minutes.
Barcelona, one of the favourites to win the competition, maintained their 100 per cent record this season with a 4-1 win over Galatasaray in Istanbul.
Russian international Aleksei Batrakov gave the Turkish champions the lead and they then had another goal disallowed, but Joao Cancelo equalised before half-time.
Lamine Yamal then turned on the style, setting up goals for Fermin Lopez and Anthony Gordon early in the second half, before substitute Karim Adeyemi sealed Barca's victory.
Tresoldi hat-trick
Italy-born German striker Nicolo Tresoldi scored a hat-trick, including a penalty, as Club Brugge claimed a remarkable 4-3 win away to Inter at San Siro.
Romeo Vermant got the Belgians' other goal, with Lautaro Martinez on target twice for Inter as they succumbed to a second straight European defeat.

In other games, Villarreal came from behind to beat Napoli 3-1 in Spain while RB Leipzig beat PSV Eindhoven 1-0 with a Brajan Gruda goal after Ivan Perisic failed to convert a penalty for the Dutch side.

Sporting of Portugal won 2-0 away to Lens in France with goals by Luis Suarez and Issa Doumbia, and it was a night to remember for Sabah as the rank outsiders from Azerbaijan downed Slavia Prague 2-0 in Baku.
Jamaican international Kaheem Parris and Rwanda's Joy-Lance Mickels secured their first victory in the league phase.
Wednesday's Champions League games include reigning champions Paris Saint-Germain at Manchester City and Real Madrid at Roma.

5fac96a1ff92f097: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 14 — Malaysia is moving towards multi-lane fast flow (MLFF), a tolling system that would eventually allow motorists to pay tolls without stopping at conventional toll plazas.
As part of that transition, two systems are now being introduced to motorists: PLUS’ JustGo and Touch ’n Go’s Titan Flow.
They are not quite the same thing.
JustGo is a digital toll payment system that uses automatic number plate recognition (ANPR) to identify a vehicle and charge the debit or credit card linked to the motorist’s account.
Titan Flow, meanwhile, is Touch ’n Go’s broader MLFF technology platform, combining Radio Frequency Identification (RFID), ANPR, Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) and artificial intelligence.
For now, motorists will encounter the technology mainly through Enhanced RFID lanes, rather than as a standalone service or a huge gantry on a highway called Titan Flow.
So how do these systems work, how can motorists use them, and what happens if something goes wrong?
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

JustGo is a digital toll payment system that uses automatic number plate recognition (ANPR) to identify a vehicle and charge the debit or credit card linked to the motorist’s account. — Picture by Sayuti Zainudin
JustGo
JustGo is essentially a camera-based toll payment system.
Once a vehicle is registered with JustGo, cameras at participating toll plazas read its number plate and match it to the motorist’s account.
The toll is then charged to the linked debit or credit card.
Motorists do not need an RFID tag specifically to use JustGo.
To sign up, users first download the JustGo app and register their phone number and email address.
They then have to complete the electronic Know Your Customer (e-KYC) verification using their MyKad, MyTentera or passport, including a real-time selfie and liveness check.
The next step is the electronic Know Your Vehicle (e-KYV), which requires the vehicle’s photographs and ownership documents.
A debit or credit card can then be linked to the account for toll payments.
Once everything is completed, the app should display the registered number plate and linked payment method, with the ANPR status shown as “ACTIVE”.
Users can register up to 10 vehicles.
Vehicles that are not registered in the user’s name can also be added, although supporting documents and manual approval may be required.
JustGo currently supports Class 1 vehicles, broadly covering passenger cars such as sedans, SUVs, MPVs and small pick-ups.
PLUS activated JustGo across participating toll plazas on its highways in August.
In its FAQ, it stated that JustGo is exclusively available at all lanes at all toll plazas on PLUS highways.
There are some location-specific exceptions, including the U-turn at the Tanjung Kupang Toll Plaza, while at the Bandar Cassia Toll Plaza, only RFID lanes are currently activated for ANPR.
The coverage is subject to change, so motorists should check the latest information from JustGo or PLUS before travelling.

In normal operation, the process is simple: drive into a participating lane, the camera reads the number plate, the system matches the vehicle to the registered account and the toll is charged to the linked bank card.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

In normal operation, the process is simple: drive into a participating lane, the camera reads the number plate, the system matches the vehicle to the registered account and the toll is charged to the linked bank card. — Picture by Hari Anggara
According to JustGo’s FAQ, motorists cannot simply pay cash at the exit if the linked card has insufficient funds.
It stated that drivers must ensure they have sufficient funds in their bank card before the start of their journey.
“If you are mid-way in your journey, kindly pull aside in a safe area i.e. a rest and relax area (R&R) to top-up your bank card safely,” the FAQ stated.
If the vehicle becomes stuck at a toll lane, motorists should use the intercom to seek assistance.
There is also a specific situation in which a JustGo user may see a Touch ’n Go eWallet deduction instead of a bank-card charge.

This can happen if the ANPR system fails to detect the vehicle at the previous entry point, meaning the toll cannot be charged to the linked bank card and is instead deducted from the linked Touch ’n Go eWallet.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Touch ’n Go describes Titan Flow as a next-generation MLFF platform that combines several technologies, including RFID, ANPR, LiDAR and artificial intelligence, together with open-payment capabilities. — Picture by Yusof Mat Isa
Titan Flow

Touch ’n Go describes Titan Flow as a next-generation MLFF platform that combines several technologies, including RFID, ANPR, LiDAR and artificial intelligence, together with open-payment capabilities.
In practical terms, however, motorists cannot currently download a “Titan Flow” app and start using it as a separate toll payment service.
Instead, elements of the technology are already being introduced through Enhanced RFID lanes.

Enhanced RFID still uses the physical Touch ’n Go RFID tag attached to the vehicle. Existing RFID tags can be used, meaning motorists do not need to obtain a special “Titan Flow” or “enhanced RFID” tag.
The basic process remains familiar to existing RFID users: obtain a Touch ’n Go RFID tag, register and activate it with the vehicle and link it to a Touch ’n Go eWallet account.
When the vehicle enters an Enhanced RFID lane, the system detects the RFID tag and the toll is deducted from the linked eWallet.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
When the vehicle enters an Enhanced RFID lane, the system detects the RFID tag and the toll is deducted from the linked eWallet. — Picture by Hari Anggara

The important difference is that Enhanced RFID is part of the technology being developed towards MLFF, with additional detection and identification capabilities being tested alongside the existing RFID system.
It is just the same system as normal RFID, but the toll lane setup has been improved for faster, more reliable vehicle detection at higher speeds.
So these technological improvements could reduce the “Reverse, Forward, InsyaAllah Detect” problem at the toll booth.
For motorists, the easiest way to tell whether they are entering an Enhanced RFID lane is to look for the designated Enhanced RFID signage, including the gold star marking.

The first Enhanced RFID deployment was at the Dato Keramat Toll Plaza on the Ampang-Kuala Lumpur Elevated Highway (AKLEH), while another was subsequently introduced at the Putrajaya-bound toll plaza on the Maju Expressway (MEX).

Touch ’n Go has also announced plans for 10 more Enhanced RFID lanes by the end of 2026, covering highways including MEX, the Kajang Dispersal Link Expressway (SILK), Grand Sepadu, Guthrie Corridor Expressway (GCE) and the East Klang Valley Expressway (EKVE).
Unlike the long-term MLFF concept with no barriers, these are still designated toll lanes.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Motorists must continue to follow the lane markings and signage rather than assuming that every part of the highway has already become barrier-free. — Picture by Firdaus Latif
Motorists must therefore continue to follow the lane markings and signage rather than assuming that every part of the highway has already become barrier-free.
So, in simple terms, JustGo identifies your vehicle through its number plate and charges a linked debit or credit card.
Enhanced RFID identifies your vehicle through an RFID tag and deducts the toll from a linked Touch ’n Go eWallet.
Titan Flow is the wider technology platform that Touch ’n Go is developing for the eventual MLFF system, rather than a separate consumer app that motorists currently need to sign up for.

The two systems are part of Malaysia’s wider transition towards barrier-free tolling, but motorists do not currently have to choose between “JustGo” and “Titan Flow” as two competing nationwide payment systems.

For now, JustGo can be used at participating PLUS toll plazas where ANPR has been activated, while Touch ’n Go users can encounter the newer Titan Flow technology through designated Enhanced RFID lanes.
The eventual aim of MLFF is to remove the need for conventional toll lanes altogether, allowing vehicles to be identified and charged while continuing their journey.
e3df02bdb07de425: “We the peoples of the United Nations determined to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war.” So begins the UN Charter. Yet Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine is well into its fourth year, confirming just how far the UN has strayed from its foundational promise.

The problem is not simply that the UN has failed to stop a major war. It is that the state waging the war exercises a veto within the very body that the Charter entrusts with preserving international peace and security.

Last month, the Security Council met once again to discuss Ukraine, and once again, the world saw how Russia has turned the Soviet Union’s permanent seat, which it usurped in 1991, into a license for impunity. If ever the council tries to respond to Russian aggression, the Kremlin blocks it.

This perverse arrangement is usually described as an unfortunate but unavoidable flaw of the system. But is it? The UN has never examined how the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic (RSFSR) or its successor, the Russian Federation, acquired membership in the organisation and on the Security Council in the first place.
Yet surely this matter warrants closer scrutiny. On the basis of which documents, exactly, did Russia inherit the Soviet Union’s veto-wielding position?
The answer is remarkably thin. Article 23 of the Charter still lists the “Union of Soviet Socialist Republics” as a permanent member of the Security Council.
The Soviet Union was a founding member of the UN in 1945, as were Ukraine (UkSSR) and Belarus (BSSR). The same cannot be said for the RSFSR or the Russian Federation.

To be sure, on Dec 8, 1991, Belarus, Russia, and Ukraine declared that the Soviet Union was ceasing to exist “as a subject of international law and a geopolitical reality”; and on Dec 21, in Alma-Ata (now Almaty), the members of the new Commonwealth of Independent States, including Ukraine, expressed support for Soviet Russia’s continuation of the USSR’s UN membership, including its permanent seat on the Security Council.

But then no legal steps were taken to secure this status ever. Instead, on Dec 24, RSFSR president Boris Yeltsin sent the UN secretary-general a letter stating that the Soviet Union’s membership was being “continued” by the Russian Federation. But it is hard to assign legal weight to this letter, because no state called the Russian Federation existed when Yeltsin sent it.

Moreover, the UN Charter explains clearly what membership requires: a formal application, Security Council consideration, an assessment of compliance with Article 2, a recommendation to the General Assembly, deliberation and a vote in the assembly, parliamentary ratification of the Charter, and a deposit of the instrument of ratification with the designated authority. There is no evidence that Russia completed this process, or even attempted to begin it.

Russia’s usurpation of the Soviet seat has no comparable precedent in UN history. When the former Yugoslavia tried the same dubious manoeuvre in 1992, the Security Council (Resolution 777) unequivocally rejected its claim to be a continuing state.

Yet in December 2022, when Ukraine’s parliament and foreign ministry formally stated that Russia’s UN membership had never been properly established, the response was silence—a tacit admission that no one could offer a credible legal rebuttal.
The proper response is obvious. Russia should be stripped of the right to represent the Soviet Union, on grounds that it came to its permanent membership on the Security Council illegitimately.

Now that its usurpation of the Soviet Union’s rights has enabled it to wage a war of aggression, putting the political and legal questions of its membership on the agenda is crucial for upholding the UN’s core mission and securing punishment for the crimes against humanity committed as part of an attack on a UN member state.

The UN has at least two precedents to draw on here. The first is China. In 1971, the General Assembly adopted Resolution 2758, recognising the representatives of the People’s Republic of China (PRC) as “the only legitimate representatives of China” and removing Chiang Kai-shek’s representatives. The vote was 76 to 35, with 17 abstentions. The PRC also assumed the permanent seat on the Security Council, though Article 23 was not amended (it still refers to the “Republic of China”).
The cases are not identical. In China’s case, two governments claimed to represent a state that continued to exist. But this distinction only strengthens the case for revisiting Russia’s status.
If deciding who represented an existing state required a vote, why was the question of who would inherit the seat of a vanished state settled by a letter?
The second precedent is Yugoslavia. Here, a state had broken apart, its largest remnant declared itself the continuing state, and the UN Security Council plainly said no.

This answer was given to Belgrade but never to Moscow—not for legal reasons, but for political ones. There were no arguments to support it, and the issue was simply never brought up for discussion. Yugoslavia had neither nuclear weapons nor designs on a permanent seat.

Against this backdrop, a third instrument has acquired renewed significance since 2022: Resolution 377 (V), known as “Uniting for Peace”. Adopted in 1950, it addresses situations in which a disagreement among permanent members prevents the Security Council from fulfilling its responsibilities.

On Feb 27, 2022, the council invoked this provision to adopt Resolution 2623 by 11 votes to one, with three abstentions, calling an emergency special session of the General Assembly. Since the decision was procedural, Russia could not veto it.

But this instrument has its limits. It bypasses Russia’s veto without questioning its right to occupy the seat from which it is cast. The General Assembly can identify Russia as an aggressor, reaffirm Ukraine’s territorial integrity, condemn annexation, and recommend mechanisms for accountability.
But those decisions are recommendations. Russia retains the power to paralyse the body whose decisions are binding, even though the legality of its presence in that body has never been established.

The debate over Russia’s status must therefore be separated from the seemingly hopeless debate over Security Council reform. There is no need to abolish the veto to challenge Russia’s use of it. There is no need to rewrite the Charter to ask whether Russia is entitled to powers the Charter assigns to the Soviet Union. There is not even a need for a separate resolution. The General Assembly already has a Credentials Committee, the mechanism through which the South African delegation’s credentials were rejected in 1974.

What will happen to the Security Council if the seat is left empty? Nothing. When the Soviet Union boycotted the council from January to August 1950, the council adopted its resolutions on Korea. An empty seat is not a veto.
Some may argue that even raising the question is dangerous. Whatever Russia has done, they will say, a nuclear power must remain inside the UN, and a channel of communication must stay open.

But reviewing Russia’s status would neither end diplomacy nor invalidate every Security Council decision adopted with Russia’s participation. The question is whether diplomacy should continue to rest on a legal fiction.

The General Assembly should do what it failed to do in 1991: formally examine the legality of the Russian Federation’s representation of the former Soviet Union. The answer need not be predetermined, but the question must finally be raised.
Member states can examine Yeltsin’s letter, the Alma-Ata papers, the practice of state succession, the Charter, the precedents of China and Yugoslavia, and three decades of subsequent practice.

Russia can present its case, others can present theirs, and the General Assembly can vote. That is how a rules-based international order should work. A nameplate does not confer the right to a seat at the table. The rules do.
Denys Shtilierman, co-owner and chief designer of Fire Point, is co-founder of #unrussiaUN, the initiative group for expelling Russia from the United Nations.

d1d01aaa5144e301: Anthropic's Claude models have been emitting so much code that the company's coding infrastructure hasn't been able to keep up. It's a symptom of the AI coding imperative and all-you-can-eat inference. Microsoft's GitHub in April published a blog post attributing recent availability problems to the exponential growth in pull requests and commits. The code flood has been noted by academic researchers, among others. For Anthropic, writing code is no longer a productivity bottleneck. Instead, the problem is managing the code after it's written, via source control, the build system, and continuous integration. "In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day," the biz said in a blog post on Tuesday. "We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce." After several months of model prompting and five months of migration, the result is a homemade version control system called Scion, a monorepo scheme that sounds a bit like Subversion, Apache's centralized version control system. Anthropic is not the first organization to look beyond Git's distributed architecture toward centralized source control. Google uses Piper, a monorepo system (along with Gerrit for Git-based code reviews). Microsoft has Virtual File System for Git, formerly GVFS, to help overcome some of the scaling issues with Git. Meta has Sapling. But as the AI biz notes, Claude's code writing ability both created the situation and offered a way out through the creation of scalable code infrastructure tools – in addition to Scion, Claude helped conjure Antique (a code review interface), a code search tool, and a source control IAM system. The decentralized approach embodied by Git is the right one for most code repos, according to Anthropic. But the company's main branch weighs in at about 100 GB, with a compressed working copy at more than a quarter of that. "We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs," Anthropic said. "Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day." Even with the tools Git provides for working with portions of a codebase, Anthropic says operations proved challenging. Scion has been designed to meet the needs of AI agents, so the client leaves much of the work to the server; the source control queries are exposed via API so internal tools can respond without needing a local repo, and there's less synchronization but more need for server speed. "In Scion, the unit of work is a 'changeset,' an entry in a write-ahead log," Anthropic explains. "A changeset stores most of what you’d expect from a commit in git. But where a git commit stores a pointer to the tree, a changeset stores a list of the files that changed relative to its first parent, along with content-addressed pointers to the compressed file contents in blob storage." Work on Scion started in January, and when Claude Mythos Preview became available internally, Anthropic's code coaxers told the model to rewrite an early Git-to-Scion ingestion pipeline. The much-hyped model produced a version that used 20 times less memory and ran four times as fast. When cost is no object thanks to ample venture funding, that sort of token spending just makes sense. Anthropic's Claude jockeys appear to be taking their obsolescence in stride. According to the AI biz, company developers who worked on Scion agree that Claude writes better code than they do. But they still possess a higher-level understanding that gives them a role as naysayers. "Very often, we found that the role of the engineers was to tell Claude 'no,'" Anthropic said. "Agents will sometimes violate core system constraints to satisfy a pattern that should never have been allowed in the first place." "Just say no." As a slogan, it's timeless. And it's never been more relevant. Anthropic says its bespoke system isn't right for general use. There will be no open source release. Nonetheless, the company contends that its own code scaling problems will become commonplace in other organizations over the next few months, so it wanted to share its approach – having ample funding to pay for writing custom infrastructure tools. ®

11e83311a7c54e72: As artificial intelligence becomes more and more powerful, its ability to handle human-like tasks is undeniable. Artificial neural networks can learn to recognize images, use language, or write computer code. Like the brain’s circuits, they reorganize themselves as they learn, adjusting the strengths of their connections to improve their performance. The question for many neuroscientists is: What can these machine systems teach them about how the brain learns? And what kinds of models are likely to be the most informative? In a paper published Oct. 9 in the journal PNAS, scientists at MIT’s McGovern Institute for Brain Research and K. Lisa Yang Integrative Computational Neuroscience (ICoN) Center argue that a crucial metric for the biological plausibility of an artificial neural network’s approach to learning is the network’s ability to organize itself, without the guiding hand of a developer. They show that it is possible for an artificial neural network to build its own learning machinery. With some simple instructions about how and when connections should change, a group of randomly connected units can reshape itself into an effective information-processing network, learning from the data it is trained on. Biological learning “Current AI technology is working very well, but it doesn’t necessarily use a learning algorithm that is used by the brain,” says Qianli Liao, a K. Lisa Yang ICoN Center Postdoctoral Fellow in the labs of MIT professors and McGovern Institure members Tomaso Poggio and Mark Harnett, and co-first author of the PNAS paper with MIT Research Scientist Liu Ziyin and graduate student Yulu Gan. Liao explains that engineers design the rules about how connections change as an artificial neural network processes training data and receives feedback about its mistakes.   When it comes to training AI to do its job, the approach is powerful. But Liao and his colleagues caution that networks designed in this way may not offer much insight into biological learning. “The brain doesn't have an external designer or architect,” Liao says. “The brain has to organize itself. And we need to know how simple rules are going to make the brain organize.” The rules that reshape neural connections as an animal learns may be different in different parts of the brain, or they may change as the brain becomes more mature. Neuroscientists are working to understand how those rules work and how they might be disrupted by aging or disease — a vital step toward developing new therapies and prevention strategies. Liao points to the development of brain-computer interfaces, which aim to restore communication when the brain’s language abilities are lost or let paralyzed patients control neuroprosthetic limbs, as one potential application. “None of these can work without knowing the rules behind neuron-neuron interactions,” he says. “That’s not achievable by just designing a circuit that works very well.” An artificial neural network’s value to neuroscience should instead be judged by the extent to which it can organize itself — not just its connections, but also the machinery that adjusts those connections. Self-organized artificial learning Working with Poggio and Hartnett, Liao, Ziyin, and Gan set out to develop and validate a self-organizing computational network capable of learning. Liao explained that the network’s structure begins with multiple layers of randomly interconnected neuron-like units. Within each layer, every neuron-like component is subject to the same rules about how connections should be adjusted. “They just interact with each other using that rule, and they develop some type of behavior,” he says. The team’s network implements the kind of simple rules thought to rewire brain circuits as humans and other animals learn from their experiences. In both the brain and the machine network, for example, “neurons that fire together wire together.” In other words, when two connected neurons are activated at the same time, the connection between them strengthens.  The team showed that a self-organizing network governed by rules like these can learn to recognize patterns and classify images. They explain that in their model, learning is enabled by self-assembling motifs that emerge according to simple rules, then serve as building blocks for functional circuits. As their network learned, these motifs reorganized themselves using an optimization strategy similar to the approach built into most modern machine learning systems, called gradient descent, in which connections are gradually adjusted in response to errors in order to improve performance. Most modern AI implements gradient descent through some form of the back-propagation algorithm, which neuroscientists say is unlikely to be used by the brain. The team compared its self-organizing network to networks designed to learn in this way and found that it performed at a similar level. Connecting brains and machines Poggio says finding a biological parallel to back-propagation could trigger significant progress in both AI and neuroscience.  “If the synaptic motifs we propose are, in fact, used by the brain to do what backpropagation does for artificial neural networks, then we will have a strong connection at the level of fundamental mechanisms between artificial and natural networks — between machines and brains,” he says. Liao says a self-organizing network does not necessarily learn the same way the brain does — but it’s a critical starting point for biological plausibility.  “Self-organization is the first high-level framework,” he says. “Once we are good with self-organization as a measure, then we can talk about next thing.” While the group’s main objective is better understanding the brain, Liao says that knowledge could ultimately improve machine learning systems, too, enabling engineers to develop networks that perform better or in more human-like ways.
967d48e037c25824: The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has killed many of the industry partnerships it used to enhance security, but don't tell the organization's acting director. Speaking on Tuesday at a virtual public sector cyber resilience summit hosted by infosec firm Rubrik, Nick Andersen claimed that CISA’s public-private partnerships are the most critical aspect of his agency’s mission. “We don’t see everything. We’re not a law enforcement agency, intelligence agency, or a regulator,” Andersen said during a discussion at the summit. CISA, he added, relies on intelligence and insight not only from other government agencies and international partners, but from the private sector as well. CISA’s mission simply can’t succeed without motivating those various partners to share what they’ve seen, heard, and dealt with in order to build a comprehensive threat model. “It’s all carrots and partnerships,” Andersen added, referring to motivating partners to get on board with programs like CISA’s CI Fortify initiative for building resilient critical infrastructure. Were that actually the case, we wouldn’t really have a story to write here, but anyone who’s been following CISA’s trials and tribulations during the second Trump administration is likely to have raised an eyebrow at Andersen’s claims. Trump returned to office riding a wave of plans to cut government spending, which included massive reductions at CISA. Among the first CISA programs axed was the Cyber Safety Review Board, a public-private body set up by the Biden administration. In addition to that closure, the Trump administration also shuttered the Artificial Intelligence Safety and Security Board, Critical Infrastructure Partnership Advisory Council, National Security Telecommunications Advisory Committee, and US Secret Service Cyber Investigations Advisory Board, all bodies consisting of government and private players working together toward cybersecurity goals. Some of those bodies have since been stood up again or reformed under new names, wasting time and money that could have been better spent by cyber defenders doing things like, you know, advising CISA and other government agencies on security matters. CISA also terminated funding for and ties to the Center for Internet Security in late 2025. One of CISA’s bodies affected by the cut was the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center, a public-private partnership that shares threat intelligence and filters essential alerts down to the local government level. CISA staff has also been slashed considerably, with around a third of the Agency’s headcount, about 1,000 people, departing since Trump returned to office. CISA has since committed to rehiring around 300, but the Trump administration’s most recent budget request proposes eliminating an additional 900 positions at the agency, along with slashing nearly a billion dollars from CISA’s 2027 budget. When we asked about the apparent contradiction, CISA reached out to point us to initiatives like its reformed councils, CI Fortify, and security exercises it hosted with industry partners to test cyber resilience to point to the continued priority the agency places on its public-private partnerships. “CISA works with critical infrastructure owners and operators to assist them in securing both the physical security and cybersecurity of the systems and assets that support essential services,” an agency spokesperson told us. “Our regional teams assist industry and government partners across the country by assessing risks, helping entities bolster defenses and improve resilience, and responding promptly to threats.” But with so many outreach employees and general staff still missing, Andersen’s claims ring a bit hollow. Either the acting administrator is misrepresenting the continued importance of private industry partnerships at CISA, or he’s in denial about the state of his agency. Neither is great, especially with more budget and staffing cuts looming, and the price will be unprepared critical infrastructure. ®

8ad1969e4f569b40: MIT Lincoln Laboratory hosted the National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology (NSCEB) on Sept. 3, for a stop on its national roadshow. The event convened representatives of state organizations, defense centers, universities, technology companies, and business executives to discuss how Massachusetts' biotechnology ecosystem can strengthen national biodefense capabilities. "We have a lot to leverage in this region to advance biotechnology," said Christina Rudzinski, assistant head of the Biotechnology and Human Systems Division at Lincoln Laboratory. "Many people are already working together to push the bioindustrial sector beyond biopharmaceuticals and into a broader ecosystem across industries. This synergy is where NSCEB comes in — connecting policy to the real-world work already happening, including here at Lincoln Laboratory and across the state." Biotechnology touches many economic and defense sectors, from disease-resistant crops and lifesaving medicines to biofuels and advanced manufacturing materials. In 2022, Congress established the NSCEB to study the national security implications of this rapidly advancing field and issue policy recommendations to ensure continued U.S. leadership.  In April 2025, the 11-member bipartisan and bicameral commission released its report, calling for a minimum of $15 billion in federal investment over five years. According to the report, China is investing aggressively to dominate the field, echoing a pattern the United States has seen before in sectors such as semiconductors. "The coalition of stakeholders working in the Massachusetts biotech ecosystem illustrates how collaborative regional work will help keep the U.S. in the lead by producing exceptional innovation across all areas of biotechnology," said NSCEB Executive Director Caitlin Frazer.  Now in the final year of its three-year mandate, NSCEB is touring the country to see local biotechnology ecosystems in action. The commission will bring insights back to Washington to help members of Congress support their regions' strengths.  Advancing Massachusetts as a defense-biotechnology hub Massachusetts has identified biotechnology as a priority technology area under its Strategic Hub for Innovation, Exchange, and Leadership in Defense (SHIELD) initiative. Launched by Governor Maura Healey in October 2025 alongside $47 million of initial aligned investment, the initiative has moved with speed and at scale. This includes standing up the BioNexus program that leverages state matching funds to develop biotechnology and biomanufacturing solutions for the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command (DEVCOM). Further, Healey included a $100 million authorization for defense sector capital projects in the Mass Wins Act, an economic development bill filed in April. The bill is currently being considered by the state legislature. During the roadshow event, Ben Linville-Engler, who co-chairs the SHIELD Working Group and serves as deputy director of the Massachusetts Technology Collaborative, led a panel discussion with representatives from the Massachusetts Life Sciences Center, Business Executives for National Security, Activate, DEVCOM Soldier Center, MassChallenge, Perimeter, Center for Advanced Manufacturing, and the Massachusetts AI Hub. They are among more than 40 partner organizations participating in SHIELD.  "There is incredible convergence between economic development and national security in all domains — land, air, sea, space, cyber, and bio," said Linville-Engler, citing the state's $48.6 billion in defense-sector economic contributions last year. "Massachusetts is committed to biotechnology and national security, and not just in Boston and Cambridge but across the entire state." In July, the SHIELD Working Group submitted a report outlining steps to speed the transition of technology into deployable capabilities, strengthen the defense workforce pipeline, and reinforce the state's national security industrial base.  Lincoln Laboratory is well positioned to support these priorities. As a Department of War federally funded R&D center, the laboratory has deep knowledge of national security needs and sustained ties to academic, commercial, and U.S. government laboratories. "These attributes can help strengthen biotechnology collaborations and integrate and transition solutions across Massachusetts and New England," Rudzinski said. Scaling up biomanufacturing One project advancing this vision is the Biotechnology Scale-up Hub for Innovation, Economic Development, Labor Training, and Defense (BioSHIELD). Planned for Worcester, Massachusetts, this 200,000-square-foot biomanufacturing facility is designed to mobilize the region's defense-biotechnology sector. "BioSHIELD's mission is to accelerate breakthrough biomanufacturing solutions that strengthen national resilience, support commercial innovation, and grow the regional economy," said Edward Wack, project co-lead and principal staff in the laboratory's Biotechnology and Human Systems Division. "It will bring together industry, academia, and government to transform ideas into scalable biological products, supporting a secure and competitive bioindustrial future."  The project responds to NSCEB's call for a national network of biomanufacturing scale-up facilities, a capacity currently missing in New England, according to Wack. The facility will offer shared equipment, infrastructure, and secure laboratory space to help bridge the "valley of death" between early-stage discovery and commercial- or defense-scale production. BioSHIELD's ready-built support networks will be key to overcoming technological and regulatory hurdles, helping innovators rapidly move capabilities to market or military use.  A coalition supporting the project includes Massachusetts Biomedical Initiatives, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, Bio Base Europe Pilot Plant, and Lincoln Laboratory. It builds on a foundational effort in central Massachusetts funding the Massachusetts TechHubs program. At the event, Wack announced the coalition has signed a memorandum of understanding to formalize the partnership. Design workshops are scheduled to begin soon, ahead of funding and construction. Connecting AI and biotechnology Other discussions centered on the intersection of biotechnology and AI, another critical area for national security. Panelists represented Boston University, the University of Massachusetts Boston, Massachusetts Life Sciences Center, Parker Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, Wyss Institute, and Phicil-itate Change. They discussed challenges in collecting and disseminating high-quality, AI-ready datasets and opportunities for AI to improve biomanufacturing and therapeutics.  Closing the event, Wack called for continued collaboration as the nation moves at speed and scale to stay at the forefront of biotechnology. "At Lincoln Laboratory, we've built a strong foundation in biotechnology for more than 25 years, and it's heartening to see this level of coordinated work taking shape. It resonates with so many of us who view biotechnology as both an economic and national security imperative," Wack said.
